subsubtopic: CORPORATE BORROWINGS AWAY FROM BANKS TO LONG BOND MARKET
speechtext:
Does the government foresee a major shift of corporate borrowing away from bank loans into the long bond market in 1974 and, if so, in what dollar amounts?
806

March 25, 1974
Order Paper Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: CORPORATE BORROWINGS AWAY FROM BANKS TO LONG BOND MARKET
speechtext: In 1973 corporations relied heavily on short-term bank credit to satisfy their needs largely for working capital purposes. This was indicative of the availability of bank credit and its cost relative to the securities markets. Corporations switch their short-term borrowings between banks and the securities markets for even small shifts in the relative costs of these funds. They can be expected to switch to the money market for example, if costs there fall below the cost of bank credit. Some such shifts have already Occurred in 1974. Future shifts will depend on the relative cost of funds. As far as the long-term bond markets are concerned, it is relevant to note first that corporations have accumulated large amounts of short-term liabilities and second that corporate fixed investment is expected to be large in 1974. Taking both of these factors into account it is likely that corporations will wish to match their assets and liabilities closely and they are therefore likely to borrow larger amounts from the long-term bond markets than in 1973. The dollar amounts involved depend on a number of factors which will only emerge as the year progresses.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN POSTAL CODE
speechtext: For what reason is the Canadian Postal Code made out of a series of numbers and letters when the Postal Code used in the United States and other parts of the world is a straight, simple numbering system?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN POSTAL CODE
speechtext:
The
Canadian postal code is designed to enable the post office to sort mail mechanically down to letter carrier walks. In order to achieve this without making use of nine or ten digits it is necessary to use letters, which of course have the effect of permitting more choices.

subtopic: MARKETING OF COARSE GRAINS-POSITION OF PRODUCERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is quite wrong to suggest that coarse grains are being removed from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. Indeed, the bulk of wheat, barley and oats which have been produced in Canada will not in any way be affected by any change of policy dealing with domestic feed grains. The question of how best to market that feed grain in Canada involves not only producers but buyers of that grain across the country, and any attempt to determine the wishes of producers and consumers would have to involve both sides of the question. speakeroldname: Mr. Eldon M. Woolliams (Calgary North) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
That this House do now consider the record, objectives and programs of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs in light of the urgent needs of urban Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the scope of the motion before the House covers the whole field of urban affairs. I shall deal as objectively as I can with the programs put forward by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford), who is responsible for housing in urban Canada. I intend this afternoon to zero in on this country's housing problems and the existing housing crisis in Canada. We intend to zero in on the program which the government announced on March 13 last. The minister announced with great fanfare that $100 million is to be provided for solving the housing problems of this country. That program is to be administered by the department. To many, it seems as if the minister is going on a power binge at the expense of the taxpayer.
I think the House is aware that two thirds of our people in Canada live in an urban environment, and that urban growth continues to accelerate rapidly. Wherever we go, whether it is Halifax, Montreal, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton or what have you, urban growth continues to accelerate rapidly. The responsibility of the federal government in this field has grown with the acceleration of populations in our cities.
I must say at the outset that this minister and this government have failed to appreciate the tremendous growth of the problem existing in urban affairs and the problem of housing for the people of Canada. They have failed to accept their federal responsibility. I say federal responsibility because it is within the constitutional powers of the federal government. Indeed, they have even failed to set up a department.
Before I get into the question of housing and zero in on this demonstration program, I wish to ask whether Urban Affairs is as important a department as the Department of Justice or the Department of Consumer Affairs, because the whole ball of wax of urban affairs affects the quality of life. We know how badly the Department of Transport is being operated. This government has failed to set up a real department of Urban Affairs. It has failed to make certain that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is responsible to the departmental minister.
At the outset, I talked about this power-hungry binge. I might call it the $54,000 program. I will say why, mathematically, I say that. This program is called the urban demonstration program. The way I see it mathematically, there are 365 days in a year. This program will be operating for five years at a cost of $100 million. Five years is equivalent to 1,825 days, so if you divide 1,825 into $100 million, it means that whether the minister is awake or asleep, this program will cost $54,794 per day for five
Urban Affairs
years, yet not one house will be built for anyone in Canada as a result of that expenditure. In rough figures, the minister has agreed to spend $54,794 every day for five years on this innovation program which, I repeat, will not build one new house. May I label this program, the power bid of the minister, "The $54,000 per day plan for five years at the taxpayers expense". It is the most expensive 24 hours for fluff that has ever been designed. It is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on the people of Canada seeking shelter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Get the facts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
My friend says, get the facts. I know he is good at mathematics. When he works it out, he will find the figures to be correct.
We have today a most serious housing crisis in Canada. I wish to quote from the March 16 edition of the Toronto Star. Perhaps these facts will impress the hon. member who likes to speak while remaining seated rather than on his feet. This article on the front page of the Toronto Star puts this program in the proper perspective. I quote:
Some home prices in Metro go up by $4 every hour
We know what the minister is spending every day on a program that will not do anything. Now, we know that the price of a house for average people in Canada is going up at the rate of $4 an hour. If that is not acceleration, we have never seen acceleration.
Before dealing with this program, I want to mention some of the things we should be doing. First, our party will support a broader and more reasonable interpretation of our national constitution. When we raise the question of the housing crisis in Canada, this government hides behind the constitution. To solve the national housing crisis, the federal government must move and become more involved with the provinces to expedite the development of serviced land at a reasonable cost. This is the key. It will also bring down the interest rate. Has this land banking program which the minister refers to with such affection solved the high cost of housing? Of course, it has not.
We shall create a new department of urban affairs and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be made directly responsible to the minister and his department. We have said over and over again that we will repeal the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials to ease the cost of building supplies and inflationary pressures. This Liberal with a big "L" tax that was brought in by Walter Gordon must be repealed and repealed now. When we are the government, it will be repealed.
We will carefully examine the principle that a proportion of municipal residential property taxes and interest on home mortgages shall be deductible from a person's taxable income. In addition, we will see that comparable benefits are given to tenants. We will not set up a plan like the demonstration program that is going to cost the taxpayers $100 million. We will set up a planning secretariat of personnel from all levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal. One of the great problems is getting serviced land into operation. This involves the three levels of bureaucracy.

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
We will encourage lending institutions to put certain portions of money into housing at reasonable rates of interest. We will integrate economic programs that will bring down the rate of interest. Today, first mortgages across this land, including CMHC, range from IOV2 to 11 per cent, and in many areas second mortgages are running as high as 21 per cent. I do not think anyone could do any better.
In my opening remarks, I mentioned the housing crisis. John Doig of the Star put it this way. He is only referring to one city. Relatively speaking, the same problem exists across this land. I quote:
Housing industry sources say the average price of a new, detached house in the city and five boroughs last month was about $85,000. It was $25,000 only 10 years ago.
This government has been in office since 1968. An ordinary house for an ordinary person with an ordinary income cost $25,000 when the government took office; it now costs $85,000.
What is the government's plan? What are they doing? We had, first, a promise of great amendments to the National Housing Act which were to cure all evils and bring down the cost of housing. We were promised landbanking to cut the cost of serviced land. Land prices continue to rise in urban centres in Canada. We were promised a public and co-operative housing program to help the low income bracket people obtain shelter. Today, there are as many people seeking that kind of shelter as there were before the program was suggested in the House. We were promised a rehabilitation program for housing. I might say that our housing committee went to Montreal. That city has its own program of rehabilitating many premises for the average man. Where is the government's program?
In many cities today, less than 5 per cent of the wage earners can afford to buy a new home or a rehabilitated one. The vacancy rate is less than one per cent in Toronto. People will soon, if not now, have to place their names on a list to wait for an apartment because the same people cannot raise money for a down payment or pay the high rates of interest. When the vacancy rate is less than one per cent, what is the result? There are not only higher prices, but we will soon be in the same position as the U.S.S.R. where people place their names on waiting lists for shelter.
I will now come to grips with what I want to say. On March 13, 1974, we were promised a most novel program. We were promised a $100 million innovation planning program spread over five years, from 1975-76 to 1980-81. Let me review once again this Habitat 2000 Program. This makes one feel it will not be implemented until the year 2000, judging by the housing crisis across this country. On page 2 of the minister's statement of March 13, we find this:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this 100 million dollar fund will be used to support urban projects in many critical areas.
He said we needed to develop innovative projects to show the effective working of new methods of house design and construction, to demonstrate the feasibility of a new, low-energy, urban system, to illustrate new ways of

getting the utmost value from scarce and expensive natural resources by recycling for multiple use and applying new technology in many other critical areas such as improved public transportation and arrangements for finances, and the building and administration of new communities or renewed communities. This is what he said the program was about. This is called the innovative program. It will be concerned with new designs for houses, new types of house construction. There is to be another feasibility study concerned with low-cost energy directed to houses. They will study recycling, whatever that means-I do not know whether they intend to recycle the people, or recycle the houses or recycle a program which doesn't exist at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: How about recycling the Grits?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
This program will not build a single house for anyone in the whole of Canada. If the minister wishes to deny it, let him stand up and say so when he speaks later today. The day the program was announced I labelled it, not an innovation program, but an inhalation program. I said, then, that any minister who had the nerve and lack of responsibility to announce a $100 million program to examine the causes of the national housing crisis must have been sniffing glue. I heard the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) speak this afternoon. He said the program announced involved wrong spending at the wrong time in the wrong manner. I could not agree with him more.
A number of reports on housing have already been made public, and I shall deal with that aspect. There was a report issued by the federal task force on housing headed by a minister in the previous government, a man who had been deputy prime minister. He went across the country and made an excellent study on housing. It came to grips with the problem. When it was presented to cabinet, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) threw it into the waste paper basket and denied the basis of the recommendations. I am happy that the minister concerned resigned from a government of that kind, because it shows that someone on the treasury benches had a sense of responsibility.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Do we need a new report? We have the Dennis report, known as the Basford hidden report-we cannot find out what it is. I could use tougher language but I will leave it to your imagination, Mr. Speaker. We have had study after study. I called CMHC today. I also called my research people. They said it would take days to find out how many studies had been conducted since 1968. Take a look at some of them.
There was the study on housing in Canada, Market Structure and Policy Performance, made in 1971 by the minister then responsible for housing. There was the task force on housing and urban development in January, 1969. There was the new National Housing Act Program for 1973. There was a federal-provincial study on housing in January, 1973. There were the deliberations of the annual conference of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada which took place in January, 1973. There was a mid-Canada Development Conference involv-
March 25, 1974

ing study groups, a CMHC study on housing statistics, the annual reports of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, an interim report on a $200 million low-cost loan program for housing by a study group in May, 1971. There was a study group concerned with planning for mobile homes; a study carried out by the Canadian Council on Social Development entitled, "Housing and People", in the fall of 1973. There was a study undertaken by the architects of Canada for the government in July, 1973, paid for, like most of the others, out of taxpayers' money. And, of course, there was Habitat-the year 2000. Then there was the study on low income urban housing.
I could go on and on. I understand that the number of studies conducted in this area amount to hundreds. Yet the minister tells us he intends to spend another $100 million in the next five years on a spending binge in an effort to solve the housing crisis. I wish he would take the $100 million and do something about building shelters for those on fixed incomes who need them.

I have to ask this question, Mr. Speaker. We in the Opposition need to find out what the minister is doing. It is not easy, because he is very glib. He is a very charming minister. Why are we spending $100 million for a study? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker. The purpose is to impress the world at the meeting of the United Nations to be held in Vancouver in the minister's constituency. That is why. And do you know what we are going to tell them? We are going to say: Look at the housing mess in Canada! Please do not follow our program because we are making nothing but mistakes. Once the world sees this it will never follow the housing program which this government is following. We want to show the world why Canada's housing plan should not be followed. Do anything, but don't follow Canada. That is really what we shall be saying.
The government believes the mere fact it establishes task forces, study groups and secretariats solves the problem, but the cost of housing is still increasing, as I have said, at the rate of $4 an hour in Toronto and, relatively speaking, it will be increasing at $2 an hour somewhere else or a dollar and a half an hour somewhere else. Today, people are being burdened with debt for life. The shackles of high payments in respect of interest and principal are around their ankles. That is a situation which presently exists. Yet we are spending another $100 million to find out what the problem is. The disparity between the rich and the poor grows day by day. The heel of domestic inflation caused by the government continues to crush those on fixed incomes.
The minister reminds me of a story about a hungry donkey. He was going down the road, mile after mile, getting more and more hungry. Finally, in a desperate condition of starvation he saw on the right side of the road a pile of hay and he saw on the left side of the road a pile of hay. In his desperate condition he was struck with transfixation. He could go neither to the right, to the left, nor could he move forward. He died on the spot from starvation. That is exactly like the minister. He looks at the problem to the right. He looks at the problem to the left. And he looks at the problem ahead. But he does
Urban Affairs
nothing. He is like the little donkey who dropped dead from starvation, even though there was a pile of hay on each side of the road.

I would not say it. I said he was a charmer. I know you enjoyed my story. I labelled this program the other day as a bunch of fluff. I was misquoted in Hansard,-, Hansard reported me as saying "a bunch of bluff". I make nothing of that. I did not say "bluff" but I will accept either word. The minister has been bluffing with a bunch of fluff. The minister convicted himself in his own statement on March 13 when he said he intended to manage the program and its funds so that "the impact of innovation will be as pervasive as possible". Then, later he said:
Governments must press forward, Mr. Speaker, with immediate solutions employing proven methods ... But we must also adopt strong measures to generate new approaches ... improved technology and innovative solutions.
This minister is on a power binge at the taxpayers' expense in agreeing to spend $100 million over the next five years, a program which amounts to $54,794 each day over the next five years and does not build one house. According to the minister's own words on March 13, he is going to be in charge of this great program. He is going to see whether he can invent some new methods to solve the crisis which exists today, a crisis which has grown worse since 1968, and certainly worse since he has become minister. Mathematically, as I see this program, there are 365 days in a year, which means that over five years there are 1,825 days. Divide that figure into $100 million and the program amounts to $54,794 per day for five years. This program is not going to solve even one of the housing problems in Canada today.
Whether you label this program a spending binge on the part of the minister or not, it is going to cost the taxpayers of Canada $54,794 a day for the next five years and represents the failure of his own government. This must be the most expensive 24 hours ever. I do not know who created this program; perhaps it was the hon. member opposite who comes from Toronto. I am going to give him some facts and figures in a moment, and I have already cited some from his own riding. I want him to go to his constituents and to tell them that he is satisfied with this program, that he is satisfied with the fact that a house which 10 years ago cost $25,000 today costs $85,000. I want him to tell his constituents that when he is on the hustings during the next election campaign, which I hope will be pretty soon since Canada cannot afford any longer this sort of government.

Let me now continue in a more sombre tone and with less anger, Mr. Speaker, although you cannot help getting angry when confronted with a program like this. We believe in the principle that every Canadian should, as of right, be able to obtain and live in suitable, reasonable cost shelter with the amenities of

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
landscape. Surely, this should not present a problem in a country with as many resources and capable people as ours. Within the natural constraints of geography and necessary economic and social limitations, the aim of government policy should be to generate sufficient housing stock of various forms so that all Canadians may exercise their own freedom of choice as to the style and tenure of housing in which they live. Surely that is not too much to ask.
Several months ago I made a speech on housing, and I do not often receive the compliment of mentioned on the editorial page of the Globe and Mail. I suppose everybody likes to be paid a compliment, and I know my hon. friend opposite does. On June 13, 1973 this is what the Globe and Mail had to say about my speech in an editorial headed "Housing's roller coaster":
Land is not the biggest villain in the rising costs of housing. Interest rates are. This is true even in the urban areas and their commuter satellites, where speculation has sent land prices skywards.
Eldon Woolliams (PC, Calgary North) reduced it to simple figures for the Commons this week. An ordinary bungalow in many urban centres now costs $35,000-
Of course, Mr. Speaker, you cannot find one at that price any more; they have already gone up $10,000 since I made my speech.
-or more, he said. If the buyer puts $10,000 down and carries a 40-year $25,000 mortgage, his total cost when the mortgage is paid off, depending upon the interest rate, would be: $75,000 at 6 per cent interest; $101,000 at 9 per cent; $110,000 at 10 per cent.
At that particular time I set out many other examples and illustrations. Who today can afford to save the down payment on a house, let alone make the payments of interest and principal that are piling up? If inflation continues-I think any Canadian can understand this, you do not have to be a high blown economist- and the cost of housing continues to rise, there will be the largest number of foreclosures in Canada that this country has ever seen, even outdoing the thirties. Surely, somebody in the department can come up with a better plan than wasting $100 million of the taxpayers' money.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week we had a public confession by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) that the national transportation policy was a mess. Today we should have the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) getting up and saying that the housing policies of the federal government are a hell of a mess. They are a tragedy, a disaster.
The motion now before the House asks us to consider the record, objectives and programs of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs in light of the urgent needs of urban Canada. To put it mildly, the record is pitiful; the objectives are based-wrongly-on the profit oriented motive, with reliance on the private sector, and the programs have certainly been meagre. I charge the Minister of State for Urban Affairs with lack of leadership and assistance in solving Canada's number one problem, housing. For months we have seen housing costs, including cost of land, mortgage interest rates and building materials, reach their highest peak and, in fact, become the highest costing component in the cost of living index across this country.

What has the Minister of State for Urban Affairs done, Mr. Speaker? He has done nothing. I looked at the Speech from the Throne but there was not one word about the housing problem in Canada. There was not one mention of bringing forth legislation to deal with the housing problem. All he has done has been to make a statement last week with regard to an urban demonstration program, spending, as my hon. friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has said, $100 million over a period of five years.
Let me tell the House that this is only a retread of the special innovative program that the government set forth in 1971, the result of which, after an analysis conducted by an independent authority, proved that we were making smaller homes on smaller lots. That was the result of the program in 1971, and when I read the details of the urban demonstration program of 1974, I have the same feeling about it as I had about the other program. This reminds me of a constituent who owned one of these small homes on a small lot. He said to me: "You know, I am going to spend the rest of eternity in a small box and the federal government wants me to spend my days on earth in the same place". I felt that was so true.
All these measures are like giving a starving elephant a peanut. As I say, there is nothing in the Speech from the Throne to deal with the housing problem, and when I look at the speech from the throne delivered in the Ontario Legislature, I find the same thing-nothing. I know that Premier Davis has stated that there is no crisis in Ontario, yet we have a 23 per cent increase in the cost of housing in Ottawa and a 25 per cent increase in Toronto. At the same time, people in the lower income groups are expending half their gross incomes on housing.
When I read in the Globe and Mail this morning that the new minister of housing for Ontario, Sidney Handleman, said we must depend on the private sector, which is euphemistically called the developers, I had a sad heart and a sad feeling for the people of Ontario. In no time at all he will probably change his name from Handleman to "mishandleman" in regard to this housing problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
We in the New Democratic Party want to set forth three new programs immediately in respect of the housing crisis in Canada. First, we should have a 6 per cent limit on all new mortgages for person of moderate and low income, with a direction to the financial institution to set aside a percentage of their investment portfolios to ensure an adequate flow of mortgage money. This would indicate the financial institutions had a sense of social responsibility instead of profit-hungry motive. We would also give tax credits to people now paying more than 6 per cent interest on the mortgages they have.
I did mention very briefly the impact of housing on the cost of living. Let me set forth for you the savings people would make if they paid no more than 6 per cent interest on their present mortgages. If we consider a mortgage of $35,000 over a 25-year term at the current rate of 10!4 per cent, the monthly payment works out at $316, and of that
March 25, 1974

$316 some $295 represents interest charges. If we were to freeze mortgages at the 6 per cent rate, the monthly payments on that same house would decrease from $316 to $223. In other words, the homeowner would be saving $93 a month, or $1,116 per year as a result of that NDP scheme.
When you consider the interest payment as a separate item from the total monthly payment, the figures are even more startling. At the 10 !4 per cent interest rate the interest payment per month adds up to $295, and at the 6 per cent rate the interest payment per month would be only $175, so this would mean a saving of $120 x 12, or $1,440 to the person per year. This would have a tremendous impact on the heavy burden Canadians are carrying in respect of housing, more especially in respect of interest rates, and it would have an indirect effect on rents that are chargeable.
I can just hear the minister and some of his colleagues saying that we cannot afford to do this, that it would be improper or not right. Let me refer him to what has happened in the TransCanada Pipeline Company, that old friend of the government. It sent out a notice of its annual meeting and one of the items in the notice indicated that as of March 4, 1974 several officers of the company were indebted on account of loans in connection with the purchase of their residences. It then sets forth the names of three officers who have obtained mortgages, the highest of which was $20,000, the next $15,000 and the third $11,000. The interest chargeable on those loans was 7 per cent on one, 61/2 per cent on another and 6 per cent on the third. I suggest that the old biblical saying that those who have shall get more applies to the TransCanada Pipeline Company, particularly when we see these senior officers of that company paying those low interest rates.
I might mention that we made an investigation of this particular item because we assumed they were first mortgages, but we found out that these were second mortgages at 6 per cent, 6 Vi per cent and 7 per cent.

Surely, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs has no right to say that we cannot afford 6 per cent mortgages across the board for all Canadians, and the minister would indicate a social responsibility to all Canadian if he adopted that line.
Moving from that suggestion of 6 per cent mortgages for all Canadians, we in the NDP say there should be a federal land banking program with an immediate target of acquiring at least 50,000 acres of serviced land which the federal government should develop. It should also lend financial assistance to municipal governments in order that they might acquire and service land for building purposes. I can hear the minister say that they have programs along these lines, but these programs have not worked because the federal government has not taken the initiative. It has relied on provincial governments to pick up the programs and implement them, but they have not done so.
I was rather surprised last week when Robert Nixon, the leader of the Ontario Liberal party, made an impassioned speech during the debate on the Speech from the Throne of the Ontario government, setting forth his alarm in respect of German, Swiss, U.S., Japanese and British investors investing in land and real estate in Ontario. He
Urban Affairs
said the reason they had done this was that the 10 per cent mortgages and the capital gains law make investments very lucrative and attractive in Ontario. I hope the Ontario leader of the Liberal party has brought this to the attention of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, and I hope that minister will not only listen to that Liberal, but will act. This present minister is not a man of action, but rather a man of words.
A policy of direct loans to municipalities was a recommendation set forth in the Dennis report. That report envisaged the need for municipalities to participate in the acquisition and servicing of land to protect land costs and values. I give the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) some marks for his insistence that federal moneys be directed to municipalities along this line, but I give him no marks for his past record with regard to lifting the ceiling on CMHC rates. I give him no marks in respect of cancelling out 25-year mortgages, allowing five-year mortgages on the rollback theory. As I said, I do give him a few marks in respect of direct loans to municipalities.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
When I think of the hon. member for Trinity and his zeal when rushing across this country to solve the housing problem, almost a religious zeal, and then when I see his performance, I am really sick at heart, to put it quite mildly, Mr. Speaker.
Let me move on to the third point, which I think is very important. We must take the profit out of housing for speculators by tax changes. I am not talking about the ordinary citizen who buys a home, re-sells it and makes a profit, because he is caught in the present bind of high prices. I am talking about the land developers and building corporations which have ripped-off the Canadian public to such a great degree. It is time, in fact it is past time, to stop them. When I read the philosophy set forth in the Hellyer task force report, that all Canadians are entitled to clean, warm shelter, and when I read the principles set forth by our party and by the Canadian Social Development Council, that every Canadian is entitled to decent housing at a reasonable cost, I ask myself what has gone wrong?
Here we have set forth a principle which should be the underpinning of a housing policy in Canada. It should be the social right of all Canadians to have decent housing in the same way they are entitled to Medicare and education. What has gone wrong, because the home prices have soared out of sight. When one thinks of the city of Toronto, the average cost of a house in Toronto as at February 1, 1974 was $46,210. This represents an increase of 50 per cent in a period of 23 months. Housing has become so expensive in Toronto that only 136 NHA loans for new housing were made in 1973 out of the nearly 40,000 new units built in metro Toronto last year. The average price of that NHA house was $36,218 and the purchaser had an average income of $15,293. Because of the $30,000 ceiling on an NHA loan the act, as an instrument of home ownership in Toronto, has become virtually inoperative. With average weekly earnings at less than $150 in Toronto

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
during 1973 the dream of home ownership is virtually impossible of realization.
I could give the same story with regard to similar prices and the similar impossibility of buying homes in all major cities across the country. In fact my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) whose constituency is a fair distance from Toronto the other day told me the cost of an unserviced lot in his area is $6,000 and the cost of a serviced lot is $8,200. In my own area, a home which I could have purchased in 1962 for $26,000 sold less than a month ago for $83,000 cash. The seller went to the real estate agent to list the property and said he wanted $70,000 for it. The agent told him that he would get him more than that. The property was listed at $87,000 and sold for $83,000 cash. This is an indication of how prices have soared out of sight. It is also an indication that something must be done about it.
What would the New Democratic Party do? We would institute a 100 per cent capital gains tax in respect of people who are in the business of buying and selling real estate. In other words, we would skim off the windfall gains of the developers and building corporations. If necessary, we would impose an excess profits tax on land developers and building corporations. Third, we would implement the recommendation of the Dennis Report regarding land developers and building corporations. Back in 1971 when we had the tax reform proposals the government closed the loophole for individuals with regard to capital investment and said that no charges could be applied to this, but it did not close the loopholes with regard to corporations.
We have these land developers and building corporations charging tax deferrals, accelerated capital cost allowances, the cost of holding land which includes mortgage interest payments, municipal taxes and so forth. The result of all these tax advantages has been that companies like the Cadillac Development Corporation in Toronto had, between 1966 and 1971, earnings of $62,968,000 on which they paid taxes of $20,506. This almost reminds me of a comparison in respect of the taxes that a certain president nearby has paid in recent years. In this case, the amount is only $20,506 out of earnings of $62 million. Consolidated Building Corporation, also a Toronto-based firm, in July 1973 purchased 18 acres of land and 17 days later sold it at a profit of $1.5 million. This company, which prior to this was involved in extensive building of homes and development of commercial property, has now gone into the land development business. Their president said that this company is a public company in the business of making a profit. Mr. Speaker, that is not a reasonable profit; it is an unconscionable profit.
These are three areas in which the minister could act immediately with regard to the housing crisis in Canada. I hope he will call together the provincial ministers, in the same way the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has called together the provincial ministers with regard to the oil crisis, to consider the housing crisis, accept the federal responsibility and give federal leadership with regard to this important problem. I hope Canadians will not have a total lack of faith in this government, but at this stage they are certainly following that trend. Surely, the minister should assume his responsibility and see to it that he

implements his philosophy and that of most Canadians that Canadians are entitled to decent housing at reasonable cost.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to thank the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) for allowing such a debate today, since housing in Canada is a major problem.
This does not mean that there are no other problems. We are now undergoing a housing crisis as well as many other crises, namely as regards employment, unemployment, food and energy. The housing crisis is in addition to all the other crises which the government is trying to get us used to.
While listening to the speeches of the two previous speakers I noted that the housing problem exists practically throughout Canada. Few areas, cities, and municipalities are spared. Perhaps some of its causes have been unconsciously deliberate, but I note that in the province of Quebec, about ten years ago, a so-called quiet revolution began and a number of pretexts were invoked to prompt people to leave rural areas and bring them to live in the cities.
This is one of the causes of the many problems experienced in the medium and large cities. Today we must deal with those problems.
The hon. member for Calgary North asked for the elimination of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and an income tax rebate in mortgage interest on family homes. I would point out to the House and particularly to the hon. member for Calgary North that the Social Credit-ers have been demanding the elimination of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials for a few years already, and my colleague from Portneuf (Mr. Godin) has brought still another motion before the House on this subject during this session. It is motion No. 2 which reads;
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of granting an income tax rebate equal to the amount paid in mortgage interest on a family home and in municipal and educational taxes, the whole not to exceed $1,000 per year.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that Progressive Conservative and New Democrat members are not the only ones asking for tax abatements for homeowners.
The Social Credit Party of Canada leads the way in that area. We have also been demanding for very long for interest rates on loans that owners would be able to afford.
Any family in need of housing realizes today that interest rates are too high, even under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation program. In some cases, the interest rate can be lowered to 8 per cent, but even that, Mr. Speaker, is too much for some people.
Just like everybody else, we realize that for several reasons, there is a housing shortage in every Canadian region. We have failed to get enough family units under construction, particularly where a high increase in demand was foreseen. For instance, a few years ago, an important development was announced in northern Abiti-
March 25, 1974

bi, that of the James Bay hydroelectric project. That meant that many northern cities would need a far greater number of houses.
In my opinion, home builders, developers and, to some extent, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials which has an office in Val d'Or, have done everything possible to meet the demand, but to no avail, because it was much greater than the supply. The demand is still very great, Mr. Speaker, so much so that many families are wondering whether they will find suitable housing not too far from their place of work. This is a lack of foresight. There has not been adequate planning to provide enough houses in order to meet the demand. Arrangements should have been made since the programs were advertised. There was a lack of foresight. Fewer houses will probably be needed when the work is completed. A very great number of houses will be available, but it will be too late.
I am also thinking about the program announced a few days ago by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford), a $100 million program referred to a while ago by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).
Mr. Speaker, within such a program, the minister wants new initiatives. I do not think that failed in the past, I even mentioned it when the minister made his statement in the House. There would no doubt be room for other projects, but we should take advantage of those that now exist. However, there are some problems. Certain housing promoters would like housing projects called "modular housing" to be approved. If people do not need a big house at the time they are buying one, they could start with a small one and add to it later on with the modular system according to their needs.
Now the cost price of these modular houses is in accordance, I believe, with the government low-cost housing program.
One can imagine how municipalities dread the building of modular houses or any other low-cost shelters. Municipalities have to contend with services, streets, sidewalks, sewers, water pipes at costs that increase as rapidly as in any other building field.
Those municipalities must also resort to loans, the rate of interests of which also increase and are increasingly hard to get.
Those municipalities prefer the building of houses that, for the same services, will yield much more in the municipal tax field. One can understand that a $25,000 or $30,000 house will be much more profitable to the municipality than a $15,000 or $20,000 one. And the municipality does not have to spend more for building streets where are the more valuable houses.
That is why municipalities dread the building of such low-cost houses.
There is also another risk in the development of these low-cost houses, namely the mass construction of slums. In almost all our towns and cities, we are at grips with decayed houses that are almost no longer livable, and in which families on welfare must live. If we try to lower the cost of construction of low-cost houses, we might build
Urban Affairs
houses that within two or three years will look like the slums we want to replace at present.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should be careful when designing housing plans, because people want and are entitled to demand a livable house, with a minimum of comfort inside. The worse a house is built, the more difficult it is to heat it, and the less comfort there is inside.
Mr. Speaker, we must be careful, I suggest, as regards this kind of low-cost housing and provide the Canadian people with houses of an usual quality, that can be built.
I will quote one single example in this regard, Mr. Speaker. In the town of Amos, houses have been built many years ago under the so-called war time housing program. These houses had been built for low income families. In principle, these houses are still designed for low income families. But in the city of Amos, in particular,-and the same probably occurs elsewhere-one may find that families whose annual incomes exceed $12,000 and even $15,000 are living in these houses, while other working-class families, whose incomes are lower, sales clerks whose incomes are not very high, must pay a higher price to find suitable shelter while families with incomes of $12,000 or $15,000 can be allowed to live in these war time houses for $80 or $82 a month.
In my opinion, this situation should be reviewed. If we are to be fair, we must review this program that was designed for low income families, and continue to offer these benefits to low income families. Some go as far as suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that those houses built for low income families be made available to those with no income, that is those with no income other than social welfare allowances. I think those suggestions should be studied carefully by the minister so the required amendments to that program might be introduced to make housing available to those in need of them.
In his $100 million program the minister asks that new initiatives be taken. I think some have already been taken, and I wonder whether the minister is aware of some of the transformations now taking place in the province of Quebec. The same situation is probably developing along the same lines in other provinces. At least there is a movement going on now, and in the Abitibi area, the Temiscamingue area, northwestern Quebec in particular, some promoters are buying at low prices as many vacant lots as possible, divide those lots in five acre holdings and then put them up for sale. They do promotion work in the United States, in certain states, to offer those lots for sale to Americans. They also offer them to Canadians interested in buying those small lots called hobby farms. Even if today those lots are not located in towns or municipalities with the transportation and communication facilities of all sorts available today it is easy to live away from urban centres. Apparently up to now some retired or near-retirement Americans seem interested in those small land holdings. I think that initiative might have been thought in terms of Americans wanting to come and live in Canada during the nice season. I wonder if more foresight would not be called for. As was pointed out earlier by the hon. member from the NDP who spoke before me and who recognized that most lots made available for house build-

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
ing purposes were much too small I think it would be a way of extending the land, thus allowing families not only to build a home there but also to have a piece of land where to grow vegetables and flowers and space to breathe non polluted air in the summer.
Mr. Speaker, this is a step that the minister should consider and make his own. He should ask his officials to consider steps such as this one in order to find possible ways of relieving large cities, of decentralizing these living areas that are causing all kinds of problems, one of which being public transit, for instance, among a great many others.
Mr. Speaker, these are subjects that the minister should consider carefully. During these few minutes, I have been unable to give him all the information needed, but I know he can find it elsewhere to examine the feasibility of such projects all across Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this motion put forward by the Conservative party on the objectives of the government's urban policy and housing policy provides us with a useful occasion to debate these issues. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), the official spokesman of the Conservative party, of course stated that the government's urban and housing objectives as outlined in the Speech from the Throne were inadequate. I had hoped that the Official Opposition would have been at least sufficiently interested in these issues to have their official spokesman participate in the throne speech debate, rather than remain silent.

speechtext: He did.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Not on housing; the Official Opposition did not have its official spokesman speak on housing and urban policy in that debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: We were waiting for today.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
I am delighted at the reaction I am getting from hon. members opposite. Obviously, they now realize that this is a matter of such concern that they should have had their spokesman deal with it in that previous debate. But of course at that time they had not held their convention, and I presume that at the time they did not have any policy. Now, having had their convention they feel they have a policy. This is a change.
The last time we had a major debate on housing was when the National Housing Act was amended. Some 18 members of the Conservative party took part in that debate, and if one reads their speeches one will see they expressed 18 different Conservative policies.
My hon. friends opposite have put forward some suggestions. One is that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials should be removed. Naturally, Mr. Speaker, we all like to remove taxes. There is no question about that. But one would have wished that the Conservative party had given this suggestion a little more thought, at least more than expressed in their policy position as put forward today. Obviously, the principal beneficiaries of the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North would be the large industrial and commercial build-

ers, the people who put up the huge office buildings and shopping centres.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: We are not talking about them.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) says they are not talking about them. I have a copy of their policy right here. It says they are prepared for the challenge. Mr. Speaker, the Tories have prepared for the challenge by turning their backs on the twentieth century. There is no mention of this policy being restricted to housing. It is clearly stated that this will assist the developers of office buildings and shopping centres. It is the typical Tory policy of giving the greatest help to those who need it least.
To the extent that the Tories' suggestion would apply to residential construction, again the people benefiting the most would be those with the most expensive housing. That is their answer to the housing problem in Canada. Surely, the Conservatives could have suggested that the tax be removed from housing alone. Surely, we don't need to remove it from shopping centres. Surely, they could have developed a system under which rebates could be paid to those who need assistance most; but they, of course, look after their rich and wealthy friends.
This debate, as I say, allows us to review the government's urban objectives and housing policies. The objectives of my ministry can be explained very simply: they are to improve urban Canada for urban Canadians, to respond to urban problems and urban issues to the utmost of our ability. We are responding to them. This government's record in responding to the problems of urban Canada is outstanding. We are dealing with housing and, in co-operation with other governments, are tackling issues such as urban transportation. We are tackling the issue of housing in new and imaginative ways. We are taking action, and urging action by other governments and the private sector, to deal with housing issues.
The important element, as speaker after speaker in the House has made clear, in housing costs is the cost of land.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Particularly serviced land.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Yes, particularly serviced land. I am glad for the assistance of the hon. member for Hamilton West. For many reasons, not the least of which is the financial burden of residential development in most municipalities, not enough serviced land has been coming onto the market. The objective of the federal land assembly program is to correct that, to bring more serviced land onto the market fast and to help bring supply and demand more closely into balance. This calls for large scale intervention by governments through the provisions of the newly amended National Housing Act, under which funds will be made available for the assembly of land. Hon. members opposite ridicule this program. When, about one year ago, we undertook to provide $100 million a year under a five-year program for land assembly purposes, they ridiculed us. Their official position, as I recall, was that they would provide $20 million.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Who are "they"?
March 25, 1974

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
The Conservatives. As a result of the response of other governments to this offer, we exceeded our target in 1973 and were able to commit $150 million for land assembly funds in 1973. We are continuing and will continue to make substantial commitments in this area.
In order to obtain the best effect or return from this investment, I have proposed to the provinces and municipalities a set of guidelines to govern the allocation of land assembly funds. I have urged that priority and funding should be given to those projects that promise quick starts, quick development, and that will put on the market serviced lots as quickly as possible. And, although we need in this country land banks for development in five, ten or fifteen years, we are encouraging land assembly projects which will provide, as I say, for quick starts and quick development. Those are the guidelines we have given to the provinces.
Second, I have proposed that a reasonable proportion of those public land assemblies so assembled should be designated for low and modest income housing. There has been wide acceptance of these principles and these guidelines are being effectively applied with regard to our loans and commitments to provinces and municipalities. The intention of these guidelines, of course, is not only to get land onto the market quickly but to make residential development more attractive to municipalities and to remove deterrents to the opening up of residential land.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) suggested that we should accept the recommendations of the Dennis report with regard to the involvement of municipalities. I have accepted them. I wish the hon. member knew more about housing policy. If he did, he would know that at the Peterborough tri-level meeting we made it clear that the federal government would support municipalities in land assembly project. Also, just before the new year we approved, in a matter of weeks, a $9 million loan for the city of Toronto for land assembly purposes, which can be carried out a" soon as provincial consent is given. We approved at the same time a substantial loan for the city of Vancouver, to enable that city to move into the land assembly business. In a speech in Toronto this morning I repeated our eagerness and willingness to support municipalities in land assembly. Let there be no doubt: we are urging the municipalities to become involved and we have the funds with which to support them.
As with most of the housing issues, the speeding up of planned residential growth is not something which can be laid at the feet of the federal government or solved by the federal government alone. Obviously, such action involves provinces and municipalities. We are urging provinces and municipalities to take every possible step to cut through red tape and bureaucratic procedures which tend to drag out the process of land development and delay the bringing onto the market of serviced lots which are for sale.
Let me remind hon. members, while we are dealing with the question of how we should bring more serviced lots onto the market, that another tool for bringing more houses into production, that is, for the creation of new housing, and for bringing supply more nearly into line with demand is the long standing sewage treatment assistance program with which hon. members are familiar. During 1973 more money than ever before was made avail-
Urban Affairs
able by way of loans and forgiveness under that program. In addition, during this session of parliament I intend to introduce legislation which, as indicated in the Speech from the Throne, will provide assistance for trunk sewers for storm water, in cases where they are used to create new developments. This should assist municipalities in areas of new development and will help to bring more lots on stream. Storm sewers until now have not been included in the program and could be used both to increase the supply of serviced land and as an instrument for planned urban growth.
Third, as an additional means of bringing more land onto the market, we will be introducing very shortly legislation related to railroad relocation. Railroads, as you know, have influenced the patterns of Canadian cities and towns right across this country. One has only to know cities such as Vancouver, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, as well as many other smaller centres, to appreciate the amount of railroad land to be found within our urban centres. Much of that land, because of changes in transportation systems, is underutilized at present. The railroad relocation proposals would mean that much of this vast acreage of railroad land can be brought back onto stream and used for development. Much of it, I hope, can be made available quickly for housing.
Finally, let me speak of another means of bringing more urban land onto the market. I refer hon. members to the neighbourhood improvement proposals and the repair and rehabilitation sections of the National Housing Act which are to come into effect in 1974. Under the leadership of the federal government, the housing act was amended and provided legislative and financial support for those who live in older areas of our cities. The act will be effective in improving those areas in which housing has been deteriorating and going out of inventory, so to speak. As a result of federal support and federal leadership we shall be able to preserve much of that housing as good housing. Most of it will be available for low or moderate income people. That way we shall preserve the use of that urban land for the people of Canada.
These are important measures, designed to get at the heart of the housing cost problem, namely, the cost of serviced lots on the market. They are designed to bring lots onto the market. They are important measures and ought to be used to the full. The government is doing everything it can to persuade provinces and municipalities to use the funds available in order to solve the housing problem and the problem with regard to price.
The next problem to be considered is the one of distribution, that is, who has access to housing and who can get into a house. Never before, Mr. Speaker, have there been so many social instruments available to help people on low and moderate incomes obtain housing. Never before in the history of this country has there been so much help available. One could go back a long way before finding programs, even such as the public housing program, which will match the ones I want to mention.
First, there is the approved assisted home ownership program by which the federal government will subsidize people on low income, not to live in public housing and not

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
to go into rent supplement programs, all of which are good programs, but to actually assist them to buy a house as an alternative to public rental. That program is being widely used across this country. Since the program became law, we have approved such loans to more than 8,000 Canadian families. These total almost $160 million for this program. Applications are continuing to come in at a very high rate which suggests that by the end of this year the benefits of this program can be extended to a total of 18,000 families.
People across the way talk of interest subsidies and the need to help the rich by subsidizing their interest. Surely, to the extent that we can apply public monies to interest subsidization, the most effective and efficient way of doing it is through the assisted home ownership program so that that interest subsidization in fact gets directly to those whose need is the greatest.
Second, Mr. Speaker, addressing this question of distribution, I want to refer to the support we are providing to non-profit and co-operative housing organizations. Traditionally in this country we have built housing either through the private sector in accordance with the profit motive or we have built government housing-constructed and owned by the government. It seems to me there is a place in this country for what, in housing circles, has become known as the third sector. Each of the non-profit and co-operative housing sections of the act are designed to give every possible support by way of start up funds, loans and 10 per cent grants to non-profit and co-operative housing organizations.
I was at a federal provincial conference this morning on non-profit and co-operative housing. I had planned to spend the day there. I had to cut short my attendance in order to listen to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).

speechtext:
In addition to non-profit and co-operative loans and that program which has our complete support, we are continuing to fund, along with the provinces, our long standing program of public housing. In 1973, we committed to this program some $177 million. We are constantly improving the public housing program in both its physical and social aspects. It remains for many Canadian families the most suitable response to their particular housing need.
Hon. members opposite say that nothing has been done on this side. By way of conclusion, I just want to list where this government is exercising and has exercised real leadership in the urban affairs area and in housing policy. First, the support which I have just been mentioning for non-profit and co-operative groups is without precedent in this country. I am delighted to see that the provinces are following our leadership in support of nonprofit and co-operative housing groups.
We are exercising leadership in the allocation of legislation and all budgets in public intervention in the land business by way of public federal-provincial or federal-municipal land assemblies. The provinces are following that leadership.
The Tory party speaks in its pamphlet about the need for better intergovernmental relationships. We are exercising leadership in the establishment in this country of new methods of tri-level consultative processes to assure that all governments in this country, federal, provincial and municipal, are going in the same direction and addressing the same problems in the same coherent and co-ordinated way.
We are and have been exercising leadership in getting municipal governments involved in land assembly and in the support of non-profit and co-operative groups. I refer these measures to the hon. member for Broadview who criticized us in this area. We have made it very clear that those amendments to the National Housing Act allowing federal support of municipally owned non-profit housing is in fact our policy.
This morning in Toronto I made it clear that we have approved in principle a loan to the city of Toronto. It is one of the first cities to get involved in the program of municipally-owned non-profit housing. We approved that loan in principle for a major rehabilitation project in downtown Toronto. I urged this morning, and I again urge, that the municipalities of this country with provincial approval get involved in municipally-owned non-profit housing corporations.

We are exercising leadership in convincing the provinces and municipalities of this country that
March 25, 1974

unbalanced and run-away urban growth is compounding the problems that face our cities and towns. We have got to pay attention how we manage growth and the rate of growth. We have got to concentrate on how we give health, strength and growth to smaller centres to take the pressures off the Montreals, Torontos and Vancouvers, how to support those smaller centres and how to go back into the core areas of our major cities to recycle and re-use them. The hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) spoke of this very subject. We are hard at work learning in this country, taking leadership and showing how we, as a country, must manage growth if we are to solve our urban problems.
We are exercising leadership in the establishment in this country of policies of urban transportation and the development of a national urban transportation development agency. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and I are currently consulting and negotiating with the provinces toward the establishment and introduction into this House of legislation for such an agency.
We are exercising leadership in putting before the country and this parliament meaningful policies for the first time to cause the relocation, re-use and recycling of underutilized railway land.
Through amendments to the National Housing Act, we have exercised leadership in going back into our older areas of our cities through the neighbourhood improvement, rehabilitation and repair provisions of the act and conserving the older areas of many of our cities. The provinces are following this leadership by developing programs of neighbourhood improvement and rehabilitation.
Next, we are exercising leadership in the area of native and rural housing. I am glad my statement the other day on the subject was welcomed by spokesmen representing native housing and Metis housing groups across Canada. I shall be consulting with the provincial governments to ensure that where necessary federal-provincial agreement is reached to enable the policies announced by me to come into effect and be operational in time for the 1974 construction season.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in the debate on the opposition motion:
That this House do now consider the record, objectives and programs of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs in light of the urgent needs of urban Canada.
I think we are all aware, Mr. Speaker, of the serious situation which exists in many of our larger cities in connection with the lack of adequate and proper housing. It may seem naive and presumptuous of me, representing a rural riding, to speak on the needs of urban Canada. Two-thirds of all Canadians now live in the cities, and urban growth continues to increase rapidly every day. Our party supports the principle that every Canadian should, as a right, be able to live in suitable accommodation at a reasonable cost.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) announced on Wednesday, March 13, his new $100 million urban demonstration program designed to find solutions to urban problems. This fund is to support urban projects in critical areas. He also stresses new methods of house design and house construction, and new ways of getting the top value from scarce and expensive natural resources. He also mentions improved public transportation. Let me emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that improved public transportation would certainly help housing problems, especially in our two largest cities, Toronto and Montreal. Faster and better train service would enable housing to be built in areas where land is available and not nearly as expensive. In Toronto now, as an example, developers do not bat an eye in asking $35,000 for a small lot.
In theory, and on paper, this program sounds excellent. However, the plan, with its $100 million expenditure over five years, will not build one additional house in Canada. The crying need at the present time and in the foreseeable future is for cheaper land, cheaper houses and, more important, cheaper mortgage money. I believe at the present time it is estimated that only four per cent of the people living in metropolitan Toronto will be able to afford to purchase a home, and only five per cent of the people living elsewhere.
I happen to be one of those rural members of parliament who advocate more housing in the rural parts of Canada to remove the pressure from the large cities. On previous occasions I have pointed out that many people now living in our larger cities, when they come to retirement age, would consider and appreciate moving Lo smaller towns or other rural areas if housing were available at moderate cost. This would provide existing housing for the many
March 25, 1974

people who work in the cities and, of course, wish to live there as well.
I am aware that there would have to be close co-operation between the municipal and provincial governments, as well as with the federal ministry of housing and urban development. I am well aware of the difficulty of getting available lots in many parts of rural Canada, especially in the province of Ontario, because of strict planning by-laws which make it next to impossible to have lots surveyed and severances approved on existing land within a reasonable period of time, if at all.
I have some doubts what this $100 million fund will accomplish. Governments in the past have had many studies made on housing, and this applies to provincial governments as well. The Dennis report on low income housing in Canada pointed out the many needs, and the Hellyer task force report on housing was also an important document. Provincial studies have been made. It all boils down to one thing: we need more and cheaper housing in all parts of Canada, not in the urban areas alone.
As for new ideas and innovations, we would all welcome some new inventions to enable houses to be built with materials other than bricks, mortar and lumber. Synthetic materials are now even more expensive, and therefore out of the question. I am wondering if some of the "brains trust" could come up with a house made out of-I will qualify it and say wind and water, and heated entirely by the sun. This may very well be possible in the future, but we are talking about housing needs today which must be met with material that is available today.
Despite the new and innovative ideas of architects, both young and old, in planning housing the cost keeps going up every day. I believe it is suggested that the cost of a house in Toronto is now increasing at the staggering rate of $4 an hour. Adding greatly to the cost of houses in many areas is the cost of municipal sewage systems. I appreciate the contributions that the federal government makes to encourage small municipalities to instal sewers, also the fact that the minister is broadening government assistance to include storm sewers and is increasing government grants. I certainly feel that in particular cases of need and high priority as far as pollution is concerned, grants should be as high as 90 per cent to enable the smaller municipalities to instal sewage systems. We know that certain provinces-Ontario, I think, is one of the leaders here-have taken advantage of this money. We are also aware that a certain province, the one to the east, has not taken advantage of the money. As a result it now has some serious pollution problems and should be forced to do something along this line.
One other priority which will greatly help increase the supply of housing is the extension of the Veterans Land Act to enable those veterans who still wish to build or purchase homes to be able to do so without any deadline. If this government expects to survive much longer, I emphasize that a statement to this effect must be made at once, and I suspect it will be made later this week. I am also hoping that the amount of available money for each veteran will be increased to at least $25,000 and that the size of the lots will be reduced to the size of ordinary building lots in cases where everything else is in order.
Urban Affairs
Our party, when we become the government, will create a new department of urban community and housing affairs which will be directly responsible for shelter. Central Mortgage and Housing will be made directly responsible to this new minister rather than continue as an independent corporation. We will also set up a planning secretariat, as mentioned by our speaker on housing, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). This secretariat will assist the officials of the three levels of government in formulating and putting into effect an imaginative and co-ordinated attack on our housing problems. With this co-operation we will be able to improve regional rapid transit systems, the location of airports, greenbelt park facilities and handle refuse collection in our large cities.
The minister mentioned that we were not interested in this sort of thing, but let me tell him that we certainly are. I am speaking for both sides of the House when I say that all hon. members are very worried and concerned about pollution. A lot of members from rural areas are a damned sight more worried than city members, because a lot of cities are trying to foist their pollution and garbage on those who live in rural areas of Canada. This garbage originated in the cities and should be disposed of there. I compliment the minister on his statement today that plants are being constructed to convert human waste so it can be used for some useful purpose. I guess he sent out an s.o.s. to that effect, to which we can say that "s.o.s." means "same old stuff". I would add another "o.s." and say "only softer". Let us hope something can be done to solve this problem.
A new and more flexible national building code must be developed, taking into consideration the regional differences and disparities. In other words, what is very necessary for the highly built up areas in large cities is not necessarily a must in the rural parts of Canada. Let me emphasize once again that our great problem has to do with the availability of money and the cost of housing. On many occasions I have recommended to the government that the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials should be abolished. I might add that previous speakers have made the same suggestion, and it has been made in parliament on numerous occasions. Let us hope that at some time in the near future this will become a reality.
The high cost of borrowing money represents one of the greatest stumbling blocks to new housing. We do not believe high interest rates are an effective way of containing inflation, and there must be lower borrowing costs for the purchasers of homes. We further pledge lower interest rates for all CMHC mortgages in line with the existing ceiling on direct loans now made by corporations to the provinces, municipalities and individuals. We also strongly support federal loans for repair, rehabilitation and improvement of existing housing. These loans should be made available to low income home owners wherever they are located in Canada.
As the head of a municipal council for a great many years, I presented resolutions on numerous occasions to municipal associations proposing that municipal property taxes be deductible from federal income tax for homeowners up to a maximum of $500. This certainly would be no
2739a-53

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
rip-off for the wealthy people. It seems unreasonable to me that a property owner should have to pay tax on tax.
There is also a great deal of merit in the suggestion that at least a portion of mortgage interest rates over 6 per cent should also be deductible from income tax. Our friends in the New Democratic Party have spoken at some length and with a great deal of feeling about the minister's proposed $100 million fund. I am just wondering how that junior partner of this coalition actually feels about this, and what that party will do when the chips are down. Certainly, if anyone has to accept the blame for what this government does or does not do, that junior partner in the lefthand corner of this House should accept at least a share. I will be interested to hear their comments in this regard at a later time. Am I to understand that they now agree with members of this party? I certainly look forward to hearing their comments.
I fully appreciate the time the minister has taken to read the coverage of that very successful and wonderful annual meeting held here in Ottawa last Monday and Tuesday. Unfortunately, he referred to policy papers, when in actual fact they were discussion papers for the 2,700 delegates who took time out in bad weather to attend this annual meeting. One can see the great support there is for this party from one end of the country to the other. I see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is listening with intense interest.
