speechtext: We are delighted to learn that this was not policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
I was pleased to hear reference by the minister to the land which is available as a result of railway relocations in the cores of towns, villages and cities. I hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will be able to apply some pressure on these railway companies with regard to the disposition of those lands.
Let me refer to one case in a small village in my riding, that famous village of Callander. The railway has abandoned its right of way in this area. The land is a useless strip for which the railway has no more use, and I am sure it acquired that land in the 1800's, just prior to the turn of the century, for something less than the staggering amount now being asked. The municipality of North Himsworth tried to buy that piece of land at a nominal rate. It is a useless strip, but the company is asking $200,000. I suggest that is absolutely ridiculous. The municipality had to settle for two or three small strategic areas, and had to pay a substantial amount for those. The rest of the land is still lying there unused.
Until I took on the full-time job of member of parliament for Parry Sound-Muskoka I was a real estate broker. When talking with one of the property men of the CNR I made a bet of one steak dinner, and perhaps I will end up having to buy it. That individual said he could guarantee me that the company would get a minimum of $175,000 for that strip of useless land. I can certainly tell you that such a price is even more inflated than other land values in the area.
I can see or understand such high prices for abandoned railway property in the centre of a large city such as Toronto, because land in those urban centres is a very expensive commodity. I am sure the railways will be

reimbursed on that basis, but surely this is not true of the hundreds of thousands of acres along railway rights-of-way in rural areas. I am certain that our friends to the left in the NDP will agree with us 100 per cent in that regard. When this land is made available, I hope it will be made available for public housing or to municipalities at a nominal rate. I am looking forward with great interest to what my friends in the NDP will have to say in this regard during the debate on this motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government places top priority on its responsibilities to urban communities and urban Canadians. It is responding now and will continue to respond to the challenge created for all of us by the conflicting manifestations of urban growth with which we have to deal, and implicit in that response is the need to maintain and improve the quality of the urban environment in our large cities and in our smaller towns and communities.
This responsibility underlies the policy development, research and co-ordination activities of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, and the housing programs of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That is why last October, at the second national tri-level conference in Edmonton, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) urged the provinces and municipalities to recognize the dangers to Canada of unbalanced, runaway urban growth. The minister suggested then that unbalanced urban growth, and the rate at which it is taking place, is one of the central issues facing all governments. At Edmonton all agreed with very little hesitation on the need for concerted action to respond effectively to urban growth. Implicit in that consensus was the need to respond to this growth in all its regional manifestations. The federal government intends to honour the commitment it made at Edmonton with speed and with effective policies and programs. The urban environment is of first priority for the federal government, and that priority is manifest in a decision taken by the federal Cabinet last summer.
In July, the Cabinet agreed to a proposal by the minister on a federal-regional goal which has two main objectives: First, to achieve a more balanced pattern of cities and towns throughout Canada with increased emphasis on support for improving small and medium size communities and for new communities where needed and, second, to improve the physical and social environment of larger urban centres, particular the core areas, or the inner city. That decision by the Cabinet last summer is one of the most fundamental that has been made by a Canadian cabinet in many years. It will take a few years for that decision to become visible, but in the long run it is going to mean a dramatic diminishing of growth in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver with a parallel increase in growth in smaller centres right across Canada. What this decision means is that federal policies and programs will be massively redirected and reshaped over the coming years to make them more responsive to the needs of an urban nation. And it means that the federal government views "urban" in the broadest possible terms, not solely in terms of Toronto or Vancouver but in terms as well of the
March 25, 1974

smaller communities and their place in the Canadian economy.
This reshaping of policies and programs affects not just the policy development activities of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs or the programs of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The commitment made by the Cabinet implies an urban redirection to the policies and programs of many departments and agencies whose activities affect the lives and future of urban Canadians. It means, further, that increasingly the federal government will join with the provinces and their municipalities to effect beneficial changes in the evolving urban future. We are already making headway in many of these policy and program areas as the Minister of State for Urban Affairs has already indicated. The amended National Housing Act, for example, has a greatly expanded potential to aid smaller communities as well as the larger centres.
The Neighbourhood Improvement Program can and will be applied to helping smaller cities as well as large ones. The Assisted Home Ownership Program has a high degree of flexibility built into it and can provide positive support for smaller cities and towns. The sewage treatment legislation, which will be introduced shortly in the House, will aid small communities as well as the large centres. The problems encountered by small towns where, because of limited population, the cost of installing sewage systems puts a very high per capita burden on the individual taxpayer will be recognized. For these communities and for others, where, because of topography, sewage costs are unusually high, additional assistance will be provided to make the program as equitable as possible across the country. It will supplement similar assistance which the provinces may provide. It will not displace such necessary support.
The national transportation development corporation, which the Minister of State for Urban Affairs proposed on behalf of the federal government at the Edmonton tri-level conference, will provide a national response to meet the cumulative need for public transportation systems and components. Such a national agency will help marshall our resources to the task of meeting current and future urban transportation demands. The proposal for a national transportation development agency was made contingent on provincial interest. That interest has been thoroughly tested in consultations across the country and everywhere a high degree of interest has been shown. The federal initiative in launching this national transportation development corporation will pay off in a number of ways, Mr. Speaker.
First, the corporation will provide a means of responding in a collective way, an integrated way, to the transportation needs of urban communities. It means that we, and not foreign entrepreneurs, will develop the systems and equipment needed to solve our urban transportation problems and not just for the large centres but, equally, for small and medium-sized centres. Second, we will be enabling Canadian companies to meet the needs of our domestic and foreign markets. This will significantly increase job opportunities as we develop export market possibilities. Third, the corporation's activities will develop and spin off new technology which will be of advantage to
Urban Affairs
other Canadian industries. Fourth, it will encourage the regional location of new transportation development and manufacturing establishments.
The domestic market for urban transportation is estimated at $5 billion to 1990. And the opportunity to develop export markets holds out an even greater economic potential. Total world demand for urban transportation system components, Mr. Speaker, are estimated at $500 billion to 1995. A strong, Canadian urban transportation capability, encouraged by this transportation development corporation, will be able to compete in that market and capture some of its benefits. Failure by the federal government to act when it did might have resulted in a degree of foreign control or influence over the development of urban transportation systems in Canada, a low level of domestic transportation development, a Canadian urban environment conditioned to foreign technology, greater regional disparity, increased importing of components and systems, and a loss of employment potential.
Mr. Speaker, the solution to our urban transportation problems will be solved in part by imaginative federal-provincial co-operation. As a result of an imaginative step by the federal government it will be solved in part by the close federal-provincial co-operation which the national urban transportation corporation envisages. This is important because we have found early on that urban problems require co-operation and consultation among governments, not competition. That accounts for the high degree of success which has accompanied the initiative of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, in establishing tri-level action committees in a number of urban communities.
In February, 1973, a tri-level committee was established for the Halifax-Dartmouth area to review plans for regional development, to further regional co-operation and to attack pressing urban problems ranging from core development and transportation to housing and land use control. A tri-level action committee is operating in Quebec City. In Ontario, the first tri-level committee at the provincial level has been developed, while special ad hoc tri-level groups have been formed to deal with regional or local issues such as the federal waterfront park in Toronto and railway relocation at Sault Ste. Marie. Railway relocation and new methods of public transit and land assembly have been studied by the tri-level group functioning since June 1972 in Winnipeg. The Vancouver tri-level committee first met in March, 1973, bringing together the three levels of government to review plans for the proposed expansion of the Vancouver International airport and to discuss a wide range of urban issues related to growth on the lower mainland.
It is through continuing action like tri-level consultation, as well as through new initiatives, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government is responding, and will respond to urban problems and the needs of the urban environment. In respect of the railway relocation legislation which we hope will appear in the House soon, the minister at the Edmonton tri-level conference last autumn in a paper delivered there indicated some of the things we can expect in the legislation. Among other things, we can expect the use of funding in order to relocate railways which run across our towns and cities and to put the land freed from railway use to more optimum use from the point of view of
27398-53J

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
the municipality concerned and also-and this seems to be missed by most people who read about railway relocation-there is a potential for using this proposed legislation for upgrading existing rail lines for rapid transit purposes such as in an area like mine, a southshore constituency opposite Montreal, which is traversed by rail lines which long ago ceased to carry passenger traffic. This proposed legislation has the potential for putting to use tremendously expensive capital facilities which are not now serving the public of Canada as they should. This legislation we are looking forward to-and members generally are extremely interested in the legislation the minister talked about at the tri-level conference last autumn- along with the energy crisis, is one of the emerging urban issues, because energy shortages will have a profound effect on the urban environment.
It is hard for us to even imagine all the effects which a fuel shortage, and all the problems that follow, will have on the way we live in cities. What we are going to see, and what we are already seeing, is a re-thinking of many wishful thoughts we all had about the future, about technological progress, about how our cities are laid out, about how we travel within and outside our own hometowns, and about the dependence we North Americans have built around machines and cars and other fuel gobblers. And, parenthetically, this development, if no other, makes our federal initiative in proposing a national transportation development corporation all that much more important.
On this continent in the past century we have thought of resources as being unlimited and have lauded anything that increased consumption, production and development. The energy crisis has challenged that ethic as has virtually no other happening. The world does not possess infinite supplies of oil and gas. The world has only a certain number of coal deposits and uranium deposits. Some experts look at this process of rethinking as another gift of the Magi. They express a rather masochistic gratitude to the oil producing countries for forcing the world to it. Rising costs of fuel, whether based on political whim or real problems in finding sources, are making some previously economically unviable sources-in Canada the obvious example being the Athabasca oil sands-feasible prospects. But whether we pay more for the already available fossil fuels or for bringing into production known reserves, the fact is we will pay more to fuel our urban system.
How should we deal with these rising costs? First, we can manipulate supply, which is the traditional approach. We can continue to search out alternate sources of conventional energy sources, or we can begin to make wider use of alternate energy sources, such as nuclear power, solar power, and so on. Second, we can manipulate demand. That is, we can force policies of conservation of energy. We can learn to change our habits and our life style.
The phenomenon of oil shortages had a pocket book impact. So, naturally, we are reacting fast. We are involved in, we read about, we take heed of advice on saving oil, inspecting the installation in our homes, putting radial tires on our cars, and staying home on Sundays. These small acts may already be having an impact on the urban environment. Already, in the city of Ottawa, the

cost of gas has contributed to changes in traffic patterns and to increased use of public transit-moves that were long needed. I think the energy crisis was the final blow to many motorists and the best of all added attractions to public transit.
In the last week or two, the government announced certain measures which would help to contribute to a solution of these energy problems that are facing our cities. The minister has alluded to them at some length in his remarks. But I feel that this reference to the official reaction of the opposition bears repeating, and I intend to repeat it not only here but elsewhere. This $100 million program which was a program not for research or for studies as opposition members have tried to make the public believe but for $100 million worth of practical projects in cities, small and large, across Canada-proposes innovation, new methods of solving problems such as ways of recycling sewage and garbage, disposal of garbage so as to produce heat for either small towns or city cores, new modes of urban living, new attacks on public transportation problems, and this is what official spokesman of the Official Opposition said:
... the government is setting up a bluff of $100 million. It is a joke.
This appeared at page 454 of Hansard.

speechtext: I support that statement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
It is to be expected that the Official Opposition would be opposed to innovation and new ideas. While that was to be expected, the amazing thing about that particular announcement was the reaction of the NDP. This is what the official spokesman of the NDP said:
I suggest in all seriousness that all this program is going to mean is $100 million down the drain . ..
When these practical projects are put into effect across Canada, it will be a pleasure for me to remind some of the recipients of what the two major opposition parties in the house said about one of the most imaginative and innovative programs that this government has announced in a long time.

speechtext: Let us build houses now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
If we are going to set about conserving energy, we can have an immediate effect on the character of Canadian cities, and the principal change will be made in public transportation. In the United States, transportation consumes about one quarter of the total energy budget of the country. More than 95 per cent of that fuel comes from petroleum. Here in Canada, 44 per cent of all petroleum products used go into transportation, and one half of that in urban areas.
It is not too far out to predict that the energy crisis will change and accelerate that change in what the experts call "urban form". It will change what the city looks like and how it is laid out. The response to the fuel situation and the need to look at means of conserving fuel over the long term will take the form of innovative urban experiments with both technology and behaviour, hardware and software, if you like. This is part of what this $100 million program is all about. We already hear of experiments with district heating in which whole blocks of homes are heated by a central plant. We hear of the possibility of whole
March 25, 1974

cities with a thermostat-climate controlled environments. I do not know whether we can do that with the $100 million program. In any event, there will be a number of practical innovative projects that will benefit Canadians from coast to coast in this venture which the minister announced to opposition laments two weeks ago.
In Canada, money has been set aside by the federal government through CMHC for provincial and municipal assembly of land for new communities, the ideal locales for some of these experiments in energy conservation and recycling. I should like to speak for a moment on the question of land assembly and the federal programs designed to deal with that matter. Let me say that since 1954 the federal government has had on its books legislation which permits federal-provincial partnerships in the ownership of land for land banking purposes, 75 per cent federal, 25 per cent provincial. Since the early '60's we have had an additional option on our books which provides for 90 per cent of the money for the cost of land assembly to be lent to a province or municipality by the federal government. These provisions, which were taken up to some extent in the 1950's, such as the Malvern project which dates back to almost 1954, is a good example of what could have been done, the potential that was there. This must be one of the major tragedies of postwar Canada-the legislation and the money were there and yet the provinces, and Ontario in particular, did not take advantage of them.
When I hear the Conservative members from Ontario, and from the Toronto area in particular, talking about what is lacking in federal housing policies, I think that if ever there was a national scandal it was the deliberate decision by the Ontario Conservative government that it would leave to private developers the development of land around Toronto, with the result that we have in the Toronto area the highest land costs in North America. This is a direct result of the lack of usage by the Ontario provincial Conservative government of legislation which has been on the federal statute books since the early 1950's.
I am surprised that the Tory opposition would even dare to propose that a day be set aside for discussion of urban problems when their party has been so deficient, not only in advancing its own policy federally but as well in the principal province where the problem occurs, and where events have shown them to be so dramatically wrong. The solution lies in the public assembly of land around Toronto for new cities, something which is provided for in our legislation. It lies in land banks. Unless this is done in much greater measure than is the case now, then not only the population of Toronto but the population of Ontario as a whole, as well as the taxpayers of Canada, will suffer.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to participate for a few moments in a debate on what I think is one of the most important questions facing governments at all levels,
Urban Affairs
a question that has faced the federal government since it assumed office in 1963. This is a debate that concerns the actions, or really the lack of actions, attributed to the federal government since it first assumed office when there was time to undo, or at least to remedy some of the situations that any vigilant government-if you are to believe its own propaganda-ought to have seen developing. It is a matter of some profound regret to me, representing an area which is largely urban, that the situation in urban Canada has been allowed to deteriorate to the extent that even this government, which as a result of its dinosaur attitude faces extinction, finally decided in 1973 that there was a problem and something ought to be done about it.
We have just had an interesting two or three weeks in this House. Last week we had the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) say that the farmer was in a bind. We had the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) make his public confession of failure. We had the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) indicate that the government has wasted millions of dollars on a computer program that is just about as unco-ordinated as the government's housing program. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) has done nothing but issue press releases about the programs which he intends to institute at some future time. Each time the cost of living index comes out the focus is turned on the failures of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). Now we have the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford), who deals with something that is just as fundamental to the development and well being of our citizens as food, and we have his record and his litany of failure with respect to housing.
It is easy to make partisan comments about the question of housing, but we have to remember the parameters within which this debate is taking place. Housing for Canadians, indeed housing for all people is a primary social, economic and physical need. It is unfortunate that we have to say these things but in Canada that need in terms of government, indeed in terms of governments in the plural sense, has been a matter of secondary consideration, at least until the federal government had its deathbed conversion in 1973. There is in fact a persistent shortage of housing across Canada in terms of the available number of units, and the shortage is growing. There is a tremendous shortage in terms of choice of housing for Canadians.
It is fair to say that sophisticated studies are not necessary to learn that there are still thousands and thousands of Canadians who are ill housed, and this includes the native peoples. It also includes the people in our cities, people in our towns, and some people in rural areas. It is axiomatic that if the government is entitled to credit for its achievements, if there are achievements, then it is also entitled to and should be condemned for its failures, and in respect of housing its policy over the years has been a monument to failure.
A few days ago the minister launched another study. His parliamentary secretary has taken great pains to say that it is not a study.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
The difference between this study and the conventional study is that in the conventional study the result comes out on a piece of paper, having been written by those who make the study, but in this particular study program the result will be in bricks and mortar, perhaps on an experimental basis, and perhaps with mistakes. If you read the minister's statement you see it is a study leading to an event that culminates in a structure in the minister's riding called Habitat 2900. A rose by any other name is still a rose. This is a study.
It was roundly condemned by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). Normally, I do not agree with the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby but I must concede that his description of it was correct. He stated, as recorded at page 454 of Hansard:
The minister said he wants this conference to be known as Habitat 2000. I suggest in all seriousness that all this program is going to mean is $100 million down the drain, of no help to people in meeting housing requirements in Canada.
That is a fairly true, fairly sound assessment of this program in the first instance. If I needed any reinforcement as to the soundness of that assessment and the truth of that assessment, it was to be found in the reaction by the parliamentary secretary to the minister a few seconds ago, he being thrust into this debate to defend the indefensible.
A little further on the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby stated:
-most of the studies that have been done have led to total inaction.
He was commenting on studies done by the department of Urban Affairs. There have been hundreds of studies undertaken by the government. Now, we have a housing situation which is supposed to respond to the clarion call given by the minister a few minutes ago. He talked about support for municipal projects, and for non-profit and co-operative groups. Why did he wait until 1973 suddenly to think of that? Does he give any forecast as to the extent of this program, how it is going to be received, and the number of units that are planned for development under it?
The minister talked about leadership in legislation and an increase in budgets. Has he indicated to the country the effects of inflation on the efficacy of those budgets? He talked about better intergovernmental relationships, and said the government was providing leadership in that field. But what do we have in this region, Mr. Speaker, close to the area which I represent? We will have them developing the so-called southeast city, the city which would be established in the township of Gloucester according to the election promise in 1972. That idea put forward by the minister and the department is not acceptable to the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton or to the township of Gloucester. The very purpose of the concept is questionable. If that is an example of this govern-

ment's leadership in intergovernmental affairs, I say it is a fraud.
The minister has provided no leadership with respect to housing. Lacking forecasts-yet being abundant with words, the minister has perpetrated a fraud on the Canadian people. Canadians have looked to the government for housing in this country. I will never forget my conversation with a young couple in an apartment building which was never meant to accommodate young families with children. In my election campaign I discovered that many people like them lived in such high-rise apartments. I will never forget what that young person said to me in Park-wood Hills. He said, "Mr. Baker, I am imprisoned in this place." He wanted to get out. He was saving money. Because the government failed to act in the field of housing, and because what it did made his dollar less valuable, he could not afford a house and found himself imprisoned. Some, of course, want to live in a high-rise and I respect their choice. But what of those who do not? What are they to do as the choices become ever more limited for more and more people? That this should be so stands as a monument to the failure of this government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Not at all. I want them to have a choice. In his speech on this motion the minister tried to defend the policies of this government. I want him to remember the young man of whom I spoke. Oh, yes, there are task forces, studies, commissions, and so on. But they will not solve the housing needs of that person. They will not answer the housing needs of the native people of this country. They will not answer the difficulties of people on lower incomes who want houses. They will not meet the needs of our senior citizens.
The time for words such as those the minister spoke this afternoon has long passed. For ten years this problem has been growing. The government has been warned, but has done nothing. For that it stands condemned. The problem has been apparent for all to see: there is the rub. I emphasize in the strongest way I can that the government ought to be roundly condemned for perpetrating against Canadians what I can only charitably characterize as a fraud.
The government has embarked upon another $100 million study or demonstration program. Let me put some figures on the record with respect to the national capital area, the area touted by the minister as a model for communities in Canada, not merely in terms of bricks and mortar but, I hope, in terms of quality of life as well as availability and choice of housing.
It is interesting to note that the average price of housing sold in Ontario rose by 26 per cent between 1970 and 1973. The price of the average Ottawa house lot rose from $5,000 in 1965 to $12,500 in 1972. The price of the average house and lot went up from $25,100 to $39,000 in the same period. The Ottawa Housing Authority, which has been involved in low-rent and limited dividend housing since 1962, has been running into increasing difficulties in every area of its operations in this period. The waiting lists for families
March 25, 1974

and senior citizens' accommodation have grown to appalling proportions.
As of December 31, 1973, 2,089 senior citizens and 1,541 families were on the Ottawa Housing Authority waiting lists. Under construction at that time were 1,643 senior citizens' units and 380 family units. With the need growing, that construction does not even begin to keep up with requirements. Without doubt, the lack of serviced lots is driving up the price of house lots and is a factor in housing costs. There is also no doubt that the situation is becoming more serious. Current housing programs at the federal and provincial levels are not integrated. If the government assures us that it is showing leadership in the field of housing, then the blame for its failure to integrate housing programs must be laid at its doorstep.
Members of the NDP sometimes suggest that reducing the mortgage interest rates would provide the answer and would make available more houses for the people of Canada. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) suggested something like this in his remarks this afternoon. With all respect, I do not think his position is correct. House prices have been forced upward primarily as a result of demand. If interest rates were lower, demand would not decrease, neither would price. I suggest that price would actually continue to increase. At first blush, it might appear that the hon. member is right; however, having given the matter much thought I do not think the NDP suggestion would reach the root of the problem, which is how to satisfy demand. Surely leadership in this field must come from the federal government, which must co-operate with provincial governments in solving the existing housing crisis. We require more co-operation.
What is the government doing? Every now and then we hear of a housing conference between federal and provincial governments. In his speech the minister said he had spoken in Toronto earlier today. He meant to imply, no doubt, that he had delivered one of his epistles inscribed on tablets of stone. I suspect the conference was improved once he left it because the question could then be discussed realistically with those in the field. There is no ongoing consultation between the federal and provincial governments. Such consultation is so necessary if we are to meet the housing needs of this country.
The minister talked about the federal home ownership assistance plan. On paper it is a good plan and the idea is good on paper. The trouble is this: it is not working effectively, particularly in the large metropolitan areas where assisted home ownership is needed. CMHC mortgage loans under this program are not forthcoming in most cities. This is the result, primarily, of the distortion in house prices. That is unfortunate as this is basically a good plan.
For example, in Chicoutimi, where the average home sells for $22,000, 204 loans were approved by the end of 1973. In Toronto, on the other hand, where the average house price is $45,000, only 27 loans were approved in the same period. In Ottawa, 40 loans were approved for the eastern Ontario region, but only 20 of those were for metropolitan Ottawa. Montreal is the exception in Canada. Housing costs there are not so high. In that city, 1,927 loans were made. The difficulty is this: in those areas where the home ownership assistance plan is important
Urban Affairs
and needed, the plan is not working. The minister should face this.
I think the real monument, or perhaps tombstone of the minister is what has happened to the consumer price index with regard to housing. In October, 1972, it stood at 145.3; in February, 1974, it stood at 159.4-an increase of 9.7 per cent. That is higher than the over-all index for all commodities and services in Canada. The figures are devastating. In St. John's, for example, there has been an increase of 8.6 per cent. That area suffers from unemployment as well. In Ottawa there has been a 7.3 per cent increase in that period of time. In Vancouver the increase has been 6.3 per cent, and in Halifax 8.7 per cent.
Those figures are really the minister's tombstone. They are the best indicator of the failure of this minister's policy. It is not all the fault of the minister because he has had some assistance in this failure. It is really the failure of the government to fight inflation and deal adequately and in a straightforward manner with this basic and fundamental problem. The housing cost figures are alarming.

Mr. Speaker, some remarks could be made before six o'clock in relation to the debate that is taking place, but before doing so and with Your Honour's permission I wish to read into the record some statements and reveal their source. They were made by a political figure. He is quoted as saying:
"What we are trying to do is expand supply; it is the old-fashioned market philosophy-if you increase supply, the price will come down and stabilize."
In relation to housing, he is also quoted as saying:
-war against speculation is twofold: public wariness, and private negotiations. In public he is giving notice that the government is going to attempt to "depress and even roll back prices," and in private he is negotiating with what he calls "the other two points in the triangle- the municipalities and the private sector."
Another quotation of interest is the announcement of a housing action program as follows:
-to increase the supply of housing available, naming areas, target dates and housing prices. The theory is that this increase in supply will depress the cost of housing ...
"A lot of this speculative boom is psychology," Mr. Handleman said. "People say you can't lose by buying land-and they've been right. What we would like to do is at least start throwing out the idea among the people who are speculating-'Hey, maybe this guy is going to put an end to this; we better start by being careful.'
"... And when the first guy says, 'No, I think I'll put my money into stocks and bonds instead of buying land and that is mutliplied several times, the market forces will begin to work. As word gets around, you can break the psychological circle, or start to, by just warning people."
These remarks were made by a person who today fills the position of minister of housing for the province of Ontario. They were published in today's Globe and Mail. An innocent bystander in the galleries today who had been listening to this debate until now would wonder what on earth is going on in this country and who is responsible for what. In this statement the Ontario minis-

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
ter of housing admits responsibility for the provision of housing in that province. This has not been put forward in one speech by the proposers of this motion, including the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I hope the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) does not misquote me. I referred to the federal responsibility within the terms and conditions of the constitution. I thought the hon. member would understand the constitution. There is some provincial jurisdiction and some federal jurisdiction. I am always fair with the hon. member and the minister. I hope he will be as fair with me as I am with him.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Just this afternoon the hon. member for Calgary North accused the federal government of hiding behind the constitution. How can he make the statement he just made, having said only three hours ago that the federal government is hiding behind the constitution? He knows very well that one of the basic reasons houses are so costly is the high cost of serviced land. Whose responsibility is that, if not the provinces'? Who is hiding behind what? Obviously there is a very important responsibility that has to be discharged by provincial governments. If it is not discharged, that is not the place to raise it and accuse the federal government of shortcomings.
A copy of the speech of the hon. member for Calgary North ought to be delivered to the Premier of Ontario: he is the person who at federal-provincial conferences in Ottawa publicly states that housing is definitely a jurisdiction for the province to preserve and protect. How can you have it both ways? Can you blame the federal government for not providing serviced land in the Toronto area, and at the same time deny the Premier of Ontario the right under the constitution to do that very job? Obviously not.
There is a lot of inconsistency of logic on the part of the Tories, particularly by the hon. member for Calgary North, whether he likes it or not. We admit that we have a responsibility in the other component in the cost of housing, namely, the cost of mortgages. For those who cannot afford it, the federal government should and is doing something about subsidizing mortgages. Under the assisted home ownership program the federal government has made a very significant step toward providing assistance to low income families, probably newly formed families, to recover a portion of the cost of mortgages.
It is becoming quite clear that the value of these programs is limited to the two areas where the cost of land and the cost of mortgages is still relatively low compared to other parts of the country. It is going to benefit small towns and certain rural areas. That is fine. However, we agree with those who say it is desirable for the federal government to introduce a plan of financing mortgages on a national basis and on a proper scale. This would permit for a limited number of years, perhaps ten, newly formed families to acquire their first house for the children and have a portion of the mortgage subsidized. This would, of course, require substantial expenditure. That is an important factor in such a policy. However, to come here and say, as did the hon. member for Calgary North, that prices in metro Toronto are high because of the federal govern-

ment's housing policy is not knowing what one is talking about.
If we do face a tight situation in Ontario, particularly in metropolitan Toronto, it is because the level of government charged with responsibility for providing serviced land has failed to take the necessary action. During the last 20 years it has failed to take advantage of the land bank provisions which have existed in federal statutes since 1954. At that time, loans are subsidized to the tune of 75 per cent. Later, the subsidy was increased to something like 90 per cent. But it is only very recently that Ontario has shown an interest in this legislation.

I do not know about other provinces. Perhaps the province from which the hon. member comes has done the same thing. It is another Tory province. The Tories, in their hunger for power, are saying one thing from one corner of their mouths and the opposite from the other corner. They are criticizing the government because of the effect of inflation on poor people in particular. Yet they are, by tradition, the chief proponents of private enterprise and in that capacity they are the first to protect the interests of the lending agencies, the trust companies and the banks. These are the people who would encourage the operations of the land speculators. It is they who quote in this House figures given by the Urban Development Institute. It is the hon. member for Calgary North and his hon. friend from Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) who speak in support of the Urban Development Institute. These are the proponents of the big interest groups. They now have the nerve to condemn the government and accuse it of causing inflation, when inflation is really caused by speculators behind the scenes.
A debate like this does, of course, tend to deteriorate when it becomes political. I am afraid I have been tempted into following the pattern set by the hon. member for Calgary North who, instead of trying to throw some light on the subject, slipped along the road of political expediency and ended by shedding as much light on this subject as a blind glow-worm attempting to find his way home in a one-way lane in Toronto. The hon. member for Calgary North is a master at confusing himself, confusing his colleagues and sometimes confusing even the press. He was at his best this afternoon.
Seriously, though, when we look at the question of housing we realize that once the political speeches have been made and the political dust has settled, we are confronted by an extremely complex problem. It is one which requires-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: A good government; a government which cares.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
I am glad to see this is beginning to hurt and that some response is forthcoming from over there. Its solution requires the co-operation of three levels of government, each of which is jealous of its independence. Second, housing is needed where there are jobs. Houses provided in areas where there are no jobs are likely to
March 25, 1974

remain empty. Thus, a housing policy is, of necessity, related to job location.
In an economy such as ours, generated chiefly by the large cities, more and more jobs are created in the principal urban centres. Effectively, the time comes when we run out of land in these urban centres and the question then arises: What do you do when you run out of a commodity which you cannot replace? Is the answer to increase the urban sprawl until, beginning in Ontario, it ends at the North Pole? The opposition tells us that cities should be contained within certain limits; that urban sprawl should not be encouraged.
The solution appears to lie in creating jobs in areas where the cost of land is still reasonably low and to which people should be encouraged to move in the expectation of finding employment. At this point, policy becomes the concern of the government at the federal level. I frankly recognize this. If we believe that every Canadian family should own a house, the answer might well lie in the policies put forward by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson): this is the department which is trying to create new jobs in less populated areas, thus relieving the enormous pressure on the larger centres.
If what I am saying is acceptable as a theory, another important role has to be played by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In addition, there is a role to be played by the Department of Finance in providing certain specific incentives. To expect that the supply of houses can be increased today by the tens of thousands in areas where appropriate land no longer exists is, in my opinion, to entertain hopes which are altogether unrealistic, unless hon. members are prepared to argue in favour of a policy of building high-rise apartments, a policy of replacing neighbourhood low-rise with high-rise structures-a policy which every sociologist has criticized as being inadequate.
Another important question is whether our policies are adequate in terms of providing housing for people with low incomes. We have been fairly successful in developing a variety of programs which meet the needs of middle income Canadians, but it is becoming clear now that the opportunities open to low income Canadians are rapidly diminishing. Housing and jobs go together. This is a subject not only for debate within the political arena; it is one which calls for creative thinking and the provision of practical alternatives, in the absence of which we shall still be debating housing when we are grandparents and great-grandparents, with extremely limited results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia)-I am sorry he is not here this evening-thought he was going to shed some light on the housing problem facing those of us who live in urban areas, and in particular the urban area known as metropolitan Toronto and its envi-
Urban Affairs
rons. Sir, he did not shed any light at all. He attempted to make an apology for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) by suggesting that the minister was not responsible for doing anything about housing, that really it was a matter for the provinces. I think all members of the House would agree that it is a matter of joint responsibility of the municipal, provincial and federal authorities, but that a great portion of that responsibility rests with the Minister of State for Urban Affairs in this parliament.
On March 13 last the minister stood in this House and made a great pronouncement. He said he was going to enter into another demonstration program. Almost like one of the famous streakers, he came forward with a new program of which he was so proud. He was going to demonstrate to all in Canada the kind of new, innovative housing that was possible today. He said that this demonstration would culminate in the creation of Habitat 2000.
The minister then sat down, and from every corner of this House opposition spokesmen said what they thought about this minister and his program, and the minister slumped further and further into his seat. This is the minister who really is responsible for nothing except sound and fury. What he says really signifies nothing. He is like Nero playing the fiddle. He is the kind of fellow who really has nothing to offer other than famous words and slogans.
Last year the minister introduced AHOP and NIP. Last week he brought to us MIC. What have they produced for the people of Canada? A great big zip. The minister of housing should be called the minister of zip, for that is what he is. This minister fiddles while the price of houses climbs and climbs and climbs. A year ago, less than 5 per cent of the people of this country could afford to buy a new, single family dwelling. Today the percentage is much less than that. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), speaking in Ontario this weekend, said that a person had to earn $23,000 to qualify for a new home in Toronto. Pretty soon only the very wealthy will qualify for a home in this country. Members of parliament cannot qualify for a new home in metropolitan Toronto even on their salary, and we are supposed to be so well paid, the leaders of the country.
We told the minister last year that there was a shortage of serviced land. We pleading with him all last session and asked him to put some money into serviced centres, transportation, water mains and sewers. We asked him to lend municipalities money, to make grants to them. But what did he do? He land banked for tomorrow. That is the kind of minister he is. "Old tomorrow", they call him.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: What about the national dream?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
I will be coming to that. A year ago when I spoke in this House about housing costs, the price of lots in my riding was $20,000. They are now up to $42,500. All the minister has done is land bank. What has he done to curb speculation in housing? The reason he has done nothing is that he and his government are responsible for the highest inflation this country has ever seen. The proof of the pudding is in the fact that this government went to the people of Canada last week with a bond issue. The bond market in this country said, "Keep your bonds. We

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
don't believe in your paper money. We don't believe in investing in bonds because we know that if we do, they will buy us nothing when we get our money back". The people of this country are looking for something more solid to put their money in.
Since this government does not care about inflation, Canadians are running out and buying real estate because at least real estate is bricks, mortar, land-something of value. The government does not care. It says, "Protect yourselves. We cannot do anything about it; inflation is a worldwide problem". People are realizing that this government does not care and they are buying real estate in order to protect their savings. So what we have now is the sort of situation that exists in my constituency, where a house which sold for $23,900 four or five years ago sold only last week for $59,500. When the house was first sold at $23,900 it bore a first mortgage of somewhere around $16,000. In the resale the new mortgage will be $40,000. The mortgage company that put up the mortgage money is a company supervised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) through the Department of Insurance.
This mortgage company is making loans to enable inflation to continue. The government is pumping money into the economy in drunken fashion so as to enable speculation in real estate to continue and roll over and over. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs does not know anything about that at all, because he does not understand that housing is purchased and sold on a low down-payment basis with huge leverage factors.
When asked what he is going to do about this problem, the minister just shrugs his shoulders and talks about land banking, AHOP, NIP and MIC. What have the minister and this government really accomplished for the people of Canada? I suggest they have accomplished nothing at all. Instead of getting down to the needs of the people and doing something about controlling financing which enables speculators to make such excessive profits, this government does nothing whatsoever.
I was in Calgary last Saturday, sitting in a coffee shop at two o'clock in the morning waiting for a flight. I met a constituent who informed me that he had purchased a house for $35,000 in March of last year and was now moving to Montreal and had sold the house last week for $54,000. That is an increase of only $20,000! He was not happy about it because he has a son who married recently and is going to buy a house. This is the kind of speculation in financing allowed by this government. This government lacks any planning in respect of control over the money supply. This is the kind of response we get from that minister across the aisle. I suggest he does not care.
Ministers over there continue to tell us that they can do nothing about inflation because it is an international problem. I suggest they cannot do anything about it because they do not want to do anything about it. At the present rate of inflation, particularly in respect of housing, it will not be very long before only the very wealthy will be able to afford accommodation, and perhaps even they will require subsidization. What hope is there in that situation?
The number of housing units being built for those of deprived circumstances in our economy, including people on old age assistance, on welfare and on widows' allowances, is far less than we require. The hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, speaking earlier today, indicated that the number of people who line up for social assistance in respect of housing is continually growing. At one time those entitled to assistance in housing could earn only a maximum of $4,000 to $5,000 a year. That maximum has now increased to $7,000 or $8,000, and I suggest that soon you will be able to qualify for social assistance in housing with a salary of $12,000. And that will eventually increase to $15,000 or $18,000, the way price structures have been rolling over and over. This government has an obligation to step in and make sure that we no longer allow increases in profits on housing to the point where homes will soon be unobtainable to all citizens.
One of the greatest problems in the housing situation can be directly related to our presently accepted methods of financing and the leverage involved. Traditionally, houses were sold with a 10 per cent or 15 per cent down payment and the balance was paid through mortgage financing. Under the present system, mortgage companies and lending institutions will lend 75 per cent of the sale price. If a house is worth $20 a square foot, a house with 1,000 square feet is worth $20,000 to build. When such a house sells for $60,000 one can only assume that the remainder represents the cost of the land. We wind up with 75 per cent financing on the total package. This leads to financing speculation on the land. The minister should realize this, and it is about time he got down to brass tacks and did something about it. I suggest we are getting no leadership from this minister, with his AHOP, NIP and MIC.
This government could not only do something about the cost of financing; it could do something about the housing shortage. The major difficulties in metropolitan areas have resulted from an acute lack of serviced land. It is all very well for the minister to say that this is the responsibility of the provinces, but with the taxing system in this country the federal authority has the taxing power and the ability to do something in this regard.
With the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, this government has an obligation to plow back at least that money into the cost of servicing land. Every brick that is laid in my municipality carries an 11 per cent tax, but the city of Mississauga does not get a dime of that back in terms of assistance toward the cost of building roads, commuter lines, water mains, parks and recreational centres to serve the people who come there. The people in my municipality throw up their hands when talking to the Ontario minister of housing. When questioned, Mr. Han-dleman always asks where the province is going to get the money for services. We all know that the province cannot print the money, like these fellows opposite us. The province must get its money legitimately.
The federal minsiter keeps telling us housing is a provincial responsibility. That is a wonderful way to duck his responsibility, which is to make it possible in areas of the country where growth is taking place to have on hand a surplus of serviced land. This could be achieved through the enormous revenues this government is obtaining from
[Mr. Blenkarn.)
March 25, 1974

the building tax; and the people who pay the building tax are in areas where the growth is taking place. I suggest that the minister could do one of two things. He could abolish the building tax and thereby reduce the cost of construction, or he could use the tax to offset the cost of servicing the land. The minister has not considered these possibilities. He thinks in terms of Habitat 2000. He thinks in terms of Habitat in Montreal, which is a marvellous demonstration of building where the wealthy can live in the downtown area. Let us have a Habitat for the ordinary guy who is trying to raise a family. Let us have a place where the ordinary man can buy a lot and build a house. I suggest the only way that can be done is by making money available for servicing land.
The minister's parliamentary secretary spoke about land banking and blamed the province of Ontario for not accepting assistance in this field. I would ask him what he proposes to do. Does he intend to go to the McLaughlin and Cadillac corporations and ask them to buy up the land, allowing them tremendous profits; or is he prepared to adopt a policy of servicing this land with the use of funds such as those created by the building tax in order that developers will not be able to speculate but will have to develop these areas in a legitimate way?
Is the minister prepared to step in and stop the speculation on vacant land? These speculators are not just the big fellows. Is he prepared to step in and say that they will be taxed to the ears for taking advantage of the ordinary citizen? I suggest he is not prepared to make a move like that. All he is prepared to do is talk about AHOP, NIP and MIC. He does not have anything new to offer. His whole concept in housing was out of date ages ago. The minister tours the countryside attending housing conferences. He has studies made and he initiates building projects through Central Mortgage and Housing. But he does not do a thing to assist the ordinary guy in his responsibility to look after his wife and kids.
A year and a half ago I knocked on many doors in apartment buildings that were not designed for people with children. Unfortunately, the children had to learn to ride their tricycles in the corridors. What has happened since then? The rent for those apartments has gone up, not $10 a month or $20 a month but in some cases $50 and $60 a month. At that time there was a vacancy rate of about 2 per cent or 3 per cent, but now it is less than 1 per cent. People are being forced to pay outrageous prices which they cannot afford, because of great speculation in housing.
It is up to the government to do something about this speculation, and not just wash its hands and say it cannot do anything about it because it is an international problem. How did housing ever become an international problem? Do we live in some far away island, in the United States, in Germany or in France? No, we live in Canada and there is enough land for all Canadians. There is more land for each person in Canada than there is in almost any country in the world. It is disgraceful for this government to say there is no place for a young family to plant its seed and grow simply because there is no serviced land with transportation arteries, water, sewage and the like.
Urban Affairs
To say it is necessary to bank land in order to put it away for some time in the future is a disgrace. The problem is right now. Young families are growing up, and they cannot afford houses. It is up to the government to do something about this problem. The government should use its funding, its taxation and resource abilities and step in and get on with it, instead of demonstrating. We have had enough demonstrating, new ideas and innovative thought. The people of my riding, and I am sure the people of all ridings of this House, want housing; they want four walls and a good roof to keep them warm in the wintertime. They want a place where they can live with their children. They want a backyard.
They do not want to hear about demonstrations and Habitat 2000, international conferences or the sending of $100 million down the drain in respect of demonstration Habitats 2000. They are not interested in these things. They are interested in the ordinary things they are entitled to have. They are entitled to have a piece of Canada, a place to plant their seed and raise their children. That is financially possible, it is economically possible and it is the responsibility of this government to produce.
