subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I sat through the whole of the hon. member's speech and do not recall hearing any constructive suggestions; but perhaps my memory fails me. I think we have a serious problem in respect of inflation. No one denies that. However, I wish we could separate the two problems. They are interrelated, but I do not think we are discussing inflation now. The fact of the matter is that year after year since I have been a member of this House, every previous prediction with regard to the number of housing starts has been exceeded.
27398-54'

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
I stood on platforms in the election of 1968 and said that if we did not have at least 200,000 housing starts per year I would not stand on an election platform for our party again. I knew we would meet this commitment. We not only met it but exceeded it. Last year there were 269,000 housing starts. Qualitatively, and quantitatively we are the best housed people in the world. This has not been accidental. I do not say it is good enough. We should be the best housed people in the world and should be doing better. However, I do not think there is anything to justify the type of comments which have been made.
When I talk about 269,000 housing starts, this was in a year when the net family formations were 130,000. So the net family formations have virtually matched the number of single family dwelling starts in Canada last year. I think that is a record. I am sorry I do not see my friend the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) here, because he picked out the ludicrous statistic about houses in the year 2000 costing $200,000. This type of thing does not get to the root of the problem. Of course there are major problems. There are major population movements which themselves involve problems. Although many of us are aware of this, the comments which appear in the paper on public consultation on population questions of the Canadian Institute of International Affairs bears repeating:
The proportion of urban population constituted 76.1 per cent of the total population in 1971. The corresponding figures for 1966 and 1961 were 72.6 and 69.6 per cent respectively. The majority of urban population live in urban centres with population over 100,000. The high concentration of population in big urban centres reflects the great transition from an agrarian, to an industrial, and now to a service-oriented economy with the dominance of commercial, professional and industrial activities. With the exception of Nova Scotia, all the provinces registered an increase in the proportion of urban population between 1966 and 1971.
So we see the situation and it is pretty obvious it is upon us. I think we must ask ourselves what the urban concept is. I think we also must ask ourselves what a home is, when we speak of price. Instead of talking about big, growing cities I think we have to be thinking in terms of urban systems. Transportation is critical to this concept. Those of us from the Toronto region I think rejoice over the decision to operate the Barrie commuter service to Toronto and also the one from Toronto to Richmond Hill. This provides an opportunity for new communities to spread out over a broad area with provincial planning. We are not splitting hairs about whose responsibility it is. We have met our responsibility. The government has allocated $500 million for the land banking of serviced land. This is half a billion dollars.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: Half a million?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
No, half a billion dollars. What has my great province of Ontario done? I have not heard about any of this money having been picked up yet. We are providing the tools to do the job. The provinces guard their prerogative jealously, and I do not quarrel with this because I believe it is a provincial prerogative. Since 1954 the federal government has paid 75, per cent of land assembly costs. One might ask where the provinces have been in this regard, because the problem is obtaining serviced land. There have been loans for sewers, low-cost loans with a 25 per cent forgiveness clause. It has applied
(Mr. Danson.l
to sanitary sewers but now applies to storm sewers, which again helps land assembly.
Where is the province of Ontario and where are other provinces on this? We are providing money, we are responding. I wager there would be more money forthcoming as soon as the provinces responded. It is the province which has the prime responsibility for the planning, for land assembly. I have not been able to get the facts, but I wager that the province of Ontario has taken some of this money. I would bet my bottom dollar that they will use it for land assembly at Cedarwood near the proposed airport site. If that is the case, I would consider it to be a misuse of funds because the Cedarwood development was committed before this fund became available. The fund is designed to open up new areas. If the province of Ontario is using this fund for Cedarwood, I would say that they are hoodwinking the people of Ontario and the people in the Toronto region. I urge my colleagues from that region to look at this very carefully. If Ontario has taken part of that fund and is using it at Cedarwood, they are misusing the fund because they would be spending that money anyway.
I would not like that to be a repetition of another development, Malvern, when people in the region had to draw lots and in some cases pay under-the-table money to even have their name considered for houses at a lower cost. What happens when one sector of the population buys housing at a lower cost than others? Who gets that right, and what right have they to resell houses which were purchased at a lower cost because of the foresight of the federal government and the delay of the provincial government? Who makes a profit on this lower-cost housing?
With the greater opportunity which is presented to the provinces by this federal funding, and the federal decision to run commuter trains north at Toronto as well as those running east and west-and I give the province full marks on getting the east-west commuter service going-their planning requirements are intense. The danger is that we will continue this sprawl which my colleague from Davenport (Mr. Caccia) mentioned. It could go right up to the North Pole, although I say at least to Lake Simcoe. That could happen if the present government of Ontario stays in office, but I do not think there is too much fear of that.
We have to open up areas for new communities, use this money for intelligent planning, for smaller communities to grow and thrive under proper plans. We should use this money to put into force the Toronto-centred region plan because, in spite of all its weaknesses, it is a reasonable plan. Frankly, I can criticize portions of it but the thrust is great. It leaves great areas for green belt, but regrettably the province narrows down the areas of the green belt just to let the hydro lines through. The plan must provide adequate recreational areas and agricultural areas. These are the important things that develop an urban system- not to concentrate people in the downtown core and make better living areas there.
I have serious doubts about central core renewal and its value. To be able to get decent single family dwellings on a decent piece of land one has to move away from the
March 25, 1974

central core because in the central cores of the cities there will be high density, high rise and very high cost or heavily subsidized housing. I am not sure that that is the route to take. If those people who want to live there persist, they must be prepared for high density, high rise and high cost. I object to subsidization for normal housing and I would rather use those funds more constructively in developing more humane communities where there is some greenery, some air and a recreational area.
My friend, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), probably has the same trouble in Calgary that we have in Toronto. The inflationary problem with respect to housing is a serious one to young people in particular. When I came out of the army I bought a house for $7,600, which at the time I thought was an awful amount. It was away up in North York, which is metropolitan Toronto now. Everybody thought I was crazy, and I did too; but I could do nothing else. It was my first house. I have traded up until I have a decent one now; a very old one, mind you, but one with which I am very happy. Now it is worth 20 times the amount I paid for the original house. But at least I had a start.
The house I bought had two bedrooms, one small bathroom and a kitchen that did not have push-button gadgets all over. It had an attached garage, but no paved driveway. It was a heck of a lot better than living in my parents' home or in an apartment, although those who choose an apartment can have it. It was enough to get a start. Now the houses we are talking about have 2'A bathrooms, finished recreation rooms, many of them have dens, libraries and are landscaped. Really, I think that is beyond our expectation. What should be our expectation? I think it is great if people can have all that if they can afford it, but we must look after those who cannot afford it.
The determining factor is the price of serviced land, because it is so expensive that you can only build expensive houses on it. If you went to see what was built as temporary housing at the agricultural farm in Ottawa during the last war, you would see that these are rather attractive houses. Over the years flowers and trees have grown around them. They are not a bad place in which to start a married life. From there you can move on to somewhere else. Neither are they a bad place to go to when you are older. I think we have lost the concept of that type of house.
Last week in my constituency, in Richmond Hill, there was a display of mobile homes. They are not really mobile; they are prefabricated homes. I was astounded to find them quite attractive. They are roomier than any moderately priced apartment I have seen. They are attractively appointed and are selling for $18,000 to $20,000. These were fully furnished. Some had a washer and dryer, all had a refrigerator and a stove, and they were very attractive. Perhaps someone would not want that for the rest of their life, but it is not a bad place in which to start or for when you are older and your family is grown.
We do not have to go after a $40,000, $50,000, $60,000 or $80,000 house. It is not everybody's right in Canada to own a mansion. This is what we are talking about in relative terms. We are talking about people who are forced to buy houses which they cannot afford and which are away above their means. We have to watch it very carefully
Urban Affairs
because cities are becoming oppressive places in which to live. There is a lot of action and excitement in them. I happened to be born and raised in Toronto and I love it dearly. I have lived in every province in Canada and in places abroad, yet I am always delighted to come home. But there is an oppressiveness in cities; and the bigger they are, the tougher they are.
There must be relief from tension. We see it here in Ottawa which on its doorstep has the Gatineau national park and is particularly favoured in that way. I stayed in Ottawa this weekend and yesterday went cross-country skiing. One can get there in 15 minutes and it is beautiful. People in Ottawa, although they have a difficult housing problem in that housing is so high-priced, can still live on a more humane scale. In the city of Toronto they have done a pretty good job of parks, but we have to keep this up. Regrettably, in Toronto we take a beautiful wooded ravine, which is a great asset, with a river flowing through it, and then we pave it to make it into the Don Valley parkway. This is very unfortunate. It helps the traffic to move but we have given up something else.
I urge the people in my province and in the area in which I live to pay greater attention to urban national parks. I believe the minister himself urged them to follow through on this initiative which brought the waterfront park to Toronto. The city of Toronto owns the Langstaffe jail farm in my constituency. It is 640 acres, sitting north of the city. I plead with the mayor of Richmond Hill, Mr. Lazenby, and the mayor of Toronto, Mr. Crombie, never to let that go for major development. They wanted to build a dome stadium on it. I opposed that. I may not have been popular with them, but I think you could do some imaginative things with that land in the form of reforestation. I do not mean a camping area but a place to grow trees so that kids from the city could go out there and see trees growing. It could be turned into a recreation area of some type. I say, let's get the trees planted. You can always cut some down if you have too many, but first get them planted. It takes time for trees to grow. They provide oxygen, and are a rejuvenating force in urban life.
Then there is talk about 18,000 acres for a major airport. Mr. Speaker, it could end up as Toronto's equivalent of the Gatineau park. Even if the airport is built, it would take up only a small portion, maybe only one quarter of those 18,000 acres. The rest could be turned into a park, with trees, streams and ponds and a recreation area. It is needed now, and if that is what this debate is all about-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: It is about housing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
It is also about urban matters and you cannot dissociate the two. What is needed now is a continued infusion of federal funds to permit the provinces to do sensible planning so that we can get lots of serviced land in urban areas upon which people can build their homes. Here I am not suggesting that these be poor homes: I mean adequate, attractive homes. People should be helped to get them. I happen to think that owning a single, detached home is part of the great Canadian ideal. Those who want an apartment can have that type of life, but the other is the Canadian ideal.

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
The fact remains that we have provided the initiative. I regret to say that the province of Ontario has been very slow in picking up that initiative. I could almost promise, Mr. Speaker, even though I do not have the authority to promise anything, that if the province of Ontario got off its seat with its new minister of housing and really used these funds to acquire land, more federal funds would be provided to follow up that initiative.
In the meantime we have a way of life second to none in the world. But as Canadians we are never satisfied. It may be recognized that on a purely material basis we do not have the highest standard of living, but we have the best way of life in the world. Surely we can all recognize that. It has not been achieved as the result of political backbiting: it has been the result of long-term planning and proper use of land. And, Mr. Speaker, the land is strong, by gosh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
The land may be strong, Mr. Speaker, but by gosh the price isn't right these days. It is always worth while to listen to the hon. member preceding oneself because often that way one can pick up a few notions. I always enjoy listening to the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson). For one thing, he did save me a task that I felt I might have to undertake following the recriminations of the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) which were so severe that I thought the minister would be totally shattered. I would like to see him shaken occasionally, but not totally shattered. Anyway, the hon. member for York North did pick him up a bit, so I do not feel obliged to rescue the minister.
I also have gratitude to express to the hon. member for York North for his suggestion, his serious suggestion, that the Toronto area needed more parkland. I totally agree with that. About a year and a half ago, during the federal election, the government saw the light. Somebody discovered that the city of Toronto did need parkland, and right in the middle of the election we had the offer of a Toronto harbour waterfront park at a cost of $30 million to $40 million. But we still have to wait to see that park manifest itself. I was down there recently, Mr. Speaker. I saw a tiny bit of lawn along a pier, and some park benches. They were not imported from Expo, so they must have been bought somewhere. But we are still waiting for the park.
There are many other areas in Toronto which need parks, and perhaps none more than the area I represent, Scarborough, and particularly my riding of Scarborough West. I know that if the minister takes a look at Scarborough West-which, by the way, is that part of Toronto just east of Victoria Park-he will say, "The hon. member for Scarborough West might have a good idea, but how can he bring it off, because most of the area is taken up by housing, or expressways, or roadways, or railways, or factories, a couple of small golf courses and a few ravines which have not been completely paved over," as the hon. member for York North remarked a while ago. "Where indeed," he might ask, "shall we build or establish a park in Scarborough West?"
I would ask him to look at a map of that part of Toronto and he will see a marvellous piece of free, green land; that is to say, land free of housing, factories and roadways. But it is not free to the people because they cannot get into it.
[Mr. Danson.1
However, Mr. Speaker, it is there, it is green, it is ready and it is available. It is known by some people in Toronto as the Toronto Hunt. I get a reaction from one of the Toronto members. I do not expect to get a reaction from western members because they do not understand what it is to ride to the hounds in a red jacket. In Toronto that kind of thing is still done-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: You're kidding!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
-metaphorically at least, and it is done in my riding which is predominantly a workingclass riding but where the upper crust of the city come out to entertain themselves on a magnificent piece of land. As a matter of fact, if you consider the whole area of Scarborough West which faces on Lake Ontario on a piece of magnificent geography, the Scarborough bluffs, it is about the only free space on the Scarborough bluffs. Yet the unfortunate part of it is that it is completely sealed off to the population of Scarborough West. This is a fairly densely populated part of the city of Toronto. I do not need to point out that the population of metro Toronto is now some 2.8 million.
As the hon. member for North York suggested a while ago, the pressure of population just cries out for recreational space, for green space, for places for trees to grow and indeed for people to go. I would suggest to the minister, were he here-but I am sure some of his colleagues are here and hearing-that there is a marvellous place in the eastern part of Toronto which could be taken over for a park. I am sure many people in Scarborough would appreciate it, although some people in the Toronto Hunt would not appreciate the insidious and practically seditious suggestion I am making here tonight. I do not know what they do in Victoria, but I suggest this is the only place in Canada where people still evoke riding to the hounds in red jackets. There are many people in Scarborough who would enjoy that initiative. Actually, some of the neighbours of the Toronto Hunt Club would not until recently have appreciated that suggestion because, naturally, the area immediately adjacent to the Toronto Hunt Club contains some relatively high-income people. They are in the Fallingbrook area.
The Toronto Hunt Club, in its disdain for the entire neighbourhood, including the Fallingbrook area, has put up a 12-foot wire fence to keep out the upper middle-class Fallingbrook residents because they are not quite good enough. The minister ought to know that the few members of the Toronto Hunt Club enjoy the freehold of this property for the paltry sum of $10,000 or $11,000 a year in municipal taxes. When you consider that they control 100 acres of choice, green, open space in an area in which people cry out for access to open spaces, that is very cheap territory.
I suggest to the minister that his ministry, on behalf of the federal government, should get in touch with the provincial government and, together with the municipality of Scarborough, purchase or appropriate in some decent and proper way the Toronto Hunt Club land so that it can be used not only by the people of Scarborough West but, as well by the people of Scarborough East-I see the
March 25, 1974

hon. member over there nodding-and also perhaps, by people as far away as York North. They, too, would like access to that magnificent body of water, Lake Ontario.
I was intrigued, when I heard the Speech from the Throne on February 27, to hear some reference to problems facing this country. The pertinent paragraph in the speech is worth reading in part. It is:
In the domain of social policy the government is playing a vital role to achieve a more balanced pattern of urban growth and to increase the quality of life in our cities in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities. Improved means of public transportation are indispensable to the achievement of these urban goals. Measures will be introduced to establish a national urban transportation development corporation to co-ordinate and market the development of required new technology in this field.
It was good to hear that reference to the problems our cities face. It was good to hear that the government is aware of the problem of urban growth. It was even good to hear that it is concerned about urban transportation. Even though members who have spoken have assailed your ears about the problem of housing, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that that problem has not gone away. However, there is an added problem. People in large urban communities do not simply face the problem of finding adequate housing; they also face the difficulty of going home to their houses and of going to work from those houses.
If you ask the people of my riding what it is they complain of most apart from high food prices, high living costs and high rentals, they will tell you that they complain most generally about transportation. You do not need to take my word for it, Mr. Speaker. The venerable and honourable Toronto Star had a survey commissioned in Scarborough a few weeks ago. It discovered that people were proud of being residents of Scarborough. Although they are part of a large urban conglomeration known as Toronto, the people of Scarborough tend to identify themselves as being from Scarborough. If asked, they say, "yes, we are from Scarborough." They mention that area instead of Toronto; whereas the people in Etobicoke, the mystical and mythical land at the far western end of our city, tend to identify themselves as Torontonians. As I say, the people of Scarborough tend to identify themselves as citizens of Scarborough. Although they like to live there, some 59 or 60 per cent of them say that their major concern is that of transportation.
I was pleased to see that the government had promised in the Speech from the Throne a national urban transportation development corporation, until I read the words "to co-ordinate and market the development of required new technology." If you study those words, what do you have? Nothing. There is nothing in the speech but phraseology, and phraseology we have had in superabundance from this government. I have listened to the speeches made by the minister and other cabinet colleagues and have heard nothing specific about the problems facing the cities except fine phraseology. Go back over the record of this session and of the previous session: yes, all the promises are there in the finest, flossiest Liberal language-but there is nothing specific.
Let me allude to one of the problems which faces major urban centres in this nation and my riding of Scarborough, the problem of transportation. This government really has had nothing to do with the major debate which
Urban Affairs
has raged in Toronto as to what system of transportation we should develop. Some of us have taken sides. I, myself, opposed the development of the Scarborough expressway. Some in my area think differently. We had an excellent report produced by Mr. Richard Soberman. He produced a report a number of years ago, for the Department of Transport, on commuter rail. His recent report came out squarely against the construction of the Scarborough expressway. It was a milestone decision. Furthermore, it was an important decision because of the alternative it proposed. It said that we in eastern Toronto should be served by what is known as light rail transit; that is, not a subway, not a heavy rail operation such as the Go train, but light rail transport.
There are several advantages to such light rail transit. For one thing, it is relatively cheap. We can build a light rail transit system extending from downtown to Guild-wood in the relatively far eastern end of Scarborough for about $85 million which, when compared with the cost of expressways, is peanuts. The light rail transit system would be flexible. It could adapt itself very well to our innercity transit system and could connect us very well with our intercity transport system. It would be flexible in a way in which no subway system can be flexible. There is much to recommend it, including the fact that the rolling stock can be produced in Canada. It is true, as Mr. Soberman points out in his report, that we would now need to buy the rolling stock from the United States because we have stopped making fast, light streetcars in Canada. Yet there is no reason why in the next two or three years we should not develop such an industry in this country. We have the plans, the capacity, the skills and the resources to produce our own rolling stock.
It is worth while pointing out to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) that if we decide to build our own rolling stock, not just for Toronto but for the other major cities, Montreal, Halifax, Winnipeg, Vancouver and other places, we would develop an extremely worth while Canadian industry which would make appropriate use of our resources and the skills of our working people. It could do this without interfering with the famous, or infamous, auto pact, depending on how you see it. There is no reason why we should not enter the field of light rail transit in this country to satisfy the transportation needs of our urban populations. For one thing, such a system is much cheaper to operate than some other systems. Light rail transit would be more efficient than the automobile in taking people to and from work and in and out of their communities.
Without going into the complicated engineering figures, we know it costs some 50 per cent more per passenger-mile to transport a person in an automobile than it does to transport the same person in public transit of the kind I have been describing. These days, particularly when we are energy conscious, we should be doing everything in our power to redirect the use of our resources in the most economic way possible and in the way which pays the most heed to conservation. This is all very well but, you might ask, "What can the federal government do? It is sitting here in Ottawa, and you are talking about something that is going on in the cities of Canada." If we

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
wanted to make urban transit more attractive, one of the best ways to do it is to make it less expensive. The federal government could, for example, dispose of the federal sales tax on diesel fuel. It could, for example, dispose of the federal sales tax on rolling stock and equipment used by our public transit systems across the country.
Let us think of it for a moment. Does it make sense for one public entity, the federal government, to tax another public entity, a municipal or provincial government, so that it in turn can tax the citizens? It is true that we have three levels of government in this country, but the citizens of this country are not split three ways. We are all dealing with the same taxpayer. Let us get out of the habit of taxing one public entity at another level, because obviously this is a silly thing to do and in fact there are huge diseconomies involved in it. To make public transit more attractive, let's make it cheaper and insist that the federal government take the steps that it can take, rather than produce mere phraseology, in order to make public transit more available, more effective and less expensive.
Are there other measures which can be taken by the federal government? I hesitate to suggest the next because it has something to do with transport, the Department of Transport and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) who has confessed to us that he is relatively powerless. We did not know that. We suspected the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) was relatively powerless and that is why he had to resort to phraseology, but we thought the Minister of Transport had power until he told us he was relatively powerless.
If we had a powerful Minister of Transport, he could say to the railroads of this country that their rights of way in the cities of Canada can be used for the development of light rail urban transit and they shall make these rights of way available at nominal cost. After all, Canadian National Railways is public property, and Canadian Pacific has been given public property. Therefore, there is no reason why they should stand in the way of our cities and municipalities. They should make these facilities available as readily and as freely as possible.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will see if I can cover the rest of this universe in two minutes. I know it is impossible, but I will try to make one point. I have heard a lot today about the need to control what is happening in our cities, the need to control urban growth. I doubt if I have heard anything of significance from either side of the House. Let me give a couple of examples of the kinds of things that worry me.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: All that in two minutes?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
I will give the worst examples. People in my area, again, stated in a recent survey that they want less growth and more parks. They are, very simply, saying that they want more of the amenities of life. They do not

want to be forced into a situation where a community is growing out of control.
In my last minute or so I want to ask the government what suggestions will be coming forward. What legislation will be coming forward to control urban growth in a serious and sensible way? What shall be done? What shall be proposed to control the depredations of the speculators? Nothing that I have heard from either side of the House. To put the matter as simply and bluntly as possible, we will not be able to control urban growth. We will not be able to see that the amenities of life are brought to the citizens of our large cities until we decide on a policy which will ensure that the major part of the land in our cities is publicly owned. As long as the main consideration and ownership of land is financial, and solely financial, private interests will be able to change the face of our communities without reference to us, the citizens, or to any level of government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is usually a pleasure to speak following the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) and the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney), but tonight it just seemed that the old coalition was back at work. They really said nothing about the serious housing problem in this country-just a lot of niceties. I notice that even the minister had to leave the chamber. It is unfortunate that the minister is not in the House, but considering the dismal failure of his department it is not surprising that he would find it opportune to be absent when so much well deserved criticism is aimed directly at him and his department.
One aspect that cannot be overlooked in this entire debate is that regardless of the location of the riding of the member who is speaking, the problem is the same. Whether the speaker be, like myself, from an urban riding in British Columbia, or from a rural riding in Newfoundland, the needs of our respective constituents are equally great. When the cost of a home is out of reach for the average Canadian, then something is drastically wrong. And, Mr. Speaker, when a wage earner must be making about $17,000 per year to qualify for a mortgage at current market prices, we are indeed facing a crisis in the housing field.
There was a time when the Canadian people could look to their elected government for guidance, assistance and leadership in an area so critical to their very well-being. The Canadian people, however, have long despaired of such policies from the government's housing minister. His mammoth bureaucratic monster has succeeded only in spending large amounts of the taxpayers' dollars. The building of this giant white elephant has not even succeeded in bringing forth the squeak of a mouse. Undaunted, however, by the past failures of his department, the minister has proposed the expenditure of $100 million as an urban demonstration project. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said, that is approximately $55,000 per day for five years.
It is typical of the minister's department that this $100 million will not actually build a single home. His department can find millions upon millions of dollars and can build bigger and bigger bureaucratic organizations. In fact, Mr. Speaker, about the only thing the minister's
March 25, 1974

department cannot do is build homes for the Canadians people.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
I will be glad to include that in my speech. The hon. member says "only 269,000 homes this year." Tell that to the people of this country who cannot find a home to buy. I, like hundreds of thousands of Canadians people, want to know when the minister is going to do the job he was elected to do. One would think that after the mistakes made in his previous portfolio, he would have learned that not only the Canadian people but his own party expect some results, however infinitely small they may be.
The Canadian people will no longer tolerate the government's policy that nothing can be done about inflation, that it is purely dependent upon international events and we will simply have to roll with the punches. While this may be convenient for various ministers of the Crown and may afford them the opportunity to hide behind the failure to come to grips will the inflationary cycle, it does nothing to alleviate the problems facing this nation, particularly in the field of housing.
There are steps which could be taken immediately if the government wished seriously to attack this problem head-on. Some of these points have been raised on numerous occasions by the leader of this party, by our housing critic, the hon. member for Calgary North, and by other concerned members of this party including myself. Mr. Speaker, let us cut out the nonsense, let us cut out the red tape, let us cut out the millions of dollars being wasted on smoke-screen, political gimmickry and let us get on with the job which the people of Canada elected us to do.
A person does not have to be a financial wizard, and economist or even a contractor to identify the problems. It would appear, however, that the only thing a person does not have to be to identify these problems is a minister of housing. Two weeks ago in this House, during the debate on the address in reply to the throne speech, I referred to an advertisement in a paper from Houston, Texas, in which was illustrated a 1,700 square-foot house selling for $22,900. Now, if houses can be built and sold in the United States at this price in one of the largest metropolitan areas, then surely they can be built here in Canada. But government interference at all levels has so tied up the housing industry that the frustrations alone are multifold.
Recent changes in the tax structure in this country have adversely affected the profitability of constructing apartments. As a result, demand for these dwelling units is far outstripping availability. With almost 99 per cent occupancy of available space, the resulting situation is a sellers' market and nothing else, and those forced to rent units have been charged all the traffic will bear. For young families, the situation is impossible. Not only must they earn substantial incomes even to qualify for a mortgage, they must also make substantial down-payments. For a young family this is not always possible. Add to this the current interest rates, and we are faced with a situation in
Urban Affairs
which the vast majority of Canadian cannot hope to own their homes.
In both the United States and in Great Britain a home owner is allowed a tax deduction in respect of interest paid on a mortgage, with the result that a far greater proportion of people are in a position to consider the purchase of a home. If the minister were serious about tackling the problems in his department, he could begin here. If the minister were serious about tackling this problem, he could immediately remove the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials.

It makes me sick to hear members on the other side criticize my party for not putting forward housing policies. We have a distinct housing policy. The government knows it might work, but they just sit back and hope the problem will go away. I think they will get a surprise, because their government will go away after the next election.

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
Mr. Speaker, these are only a few of the proposals recommended by the leader of this party in an effort to meet the most basic need of all Canadians, the need for reasonable and comfortable shelter. Certainly the minister responsible for housing cannot continue to head his department without showing some sign of progress, somewhere-anywhere.
Only a few days ago the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) referred to me in an interview as a fool because I questioned whether there was a connection between his removal as minister of consumer and corporate affairs and the scandal involving several well known British Columbia cement companies and accompanying political ties. I do not feel that his comments were warranted, I felt, rather, that they were spoken out of frustration at not being able to come up with a plausible explanation to offset what I had stated in the House. On the other hand, based on the minister's past performance in both portfolios, consumer affairs and urban affairs, some people might be inclined to wonder if the minister wasn't talking about himself, because only a fool would continue in the job which he had not been able to do properly since he began it and which it is obvious he will never be able to do properly as long as he holds it. Possibly the minister is content to be the government's court jester. I can assure him, however, that the people of this country are not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to a great deal of rhetoric today, most of it quite negative, I am afraid. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn). There seem to be more problems in his riding than in any other riding in the country. One of the solutions would seem to be to remove some of the growth which is going on around Mississauga to other parts of the country where growth is needed; for example, the maritimes, northern Ontario and the west. This would solve some of the problems experienced by members from the Toronto suburbs.
I was appalled at the reaction of the Conservative Party to the minister's announcement. I would point out that the announcement was not intended to solve all housing problems. It was intended to look into the future to see what we are going to do about housing problems then. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) was so confused that his confusion spread to the New Democratic Party. I think we should try to understand what this bill is attempting to do in the long term.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext: It is not a bill.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
It was not meant to solve all our housing problems. The amount involved is $100 million spread over five years, roughly $20 million a year. This is about 2 per cent of what is being spent on housing, so it is not a vast amount of money. The bill does not initiate research projects. The bill is for demonstration projects. Research will be going on, but that is not the purpose of the bill which will follow.
I should like to consider the urban problems of the future and see the type of world we are moving toward and ask whether we ought to carry on using the same type of urban development 20 years from now. If the answer is

no, we need to redirect our thinking and find new ways of approaching this challenge.
The urban areas of the developed world will double in about 25 years. If we continue with this growth rate in Canada-and I shall have something to say about that at another time-we are going to need about six Torontos between now and the turn of the century, though I am sure we can do better than having six Torontos, or 20 Ottawas. That gives the House an idea of the kind of growth we can expect. Therefore, I ask, is it satisfactory to continue building homes in the way we are building them now, using the same patterns, methods of building, the same techniques, building materials, and so on, in order to double the number of houses we have now? I think the answer is no.
One very serious problem being faced by the construction industry, the industry that builds our cities, our commercial buildings, houses, industrial plants, and so on, is the shortage of conventional resources. One of the west coast firms moved into Thunder Bay last year and the province gave them reserves that had already been cut over, though I do not know whether the province realized this. This company is going to have a lot of difficulty getting sufficient wood to plan its operations. In order to supply the wood required, the province asked all farmers to cut reserves to supply MacMillan Bloedel only. In other words, if you were cutting in Nipigon you would have to move your supplies to Thunder Bay, and so on. The reason for this is that we are running short of resources. Even though these resources are renewable, there is a limit, and given the kind of growth we have in the construction industry we will soon be reaching those limits.
So far as methods of construction are concerned, much has to be done here. Galbraith, in his latest book on economics, talked about the planning economy and the market economy. The best example he gave of the market economy, the best in terms of power and productivity, was the housing industry. We would never put automobiles on the road if we had to build them as inefficiently as we build houses. All kinds of new techniques are needed to develop a new housing industry, one that will function efficiently. Land development, methods of construction, building codes are all problem areas.
One of the most serious problems in the field of housing-and I am not the first to say this-is the high cost of mortgages. This is a question that must be attacked by the government and by this House. If one looks at the profits made by the banks of Canada during the last 12 months, one finds they increased by 200 per cent in some cases. This is one reason interest rates can be lowered. I suggest that part of a first mortgage, say the first $10,000, be at a lower rate than the rest and that this be established as a pattern across the country. The government should be introducing measures to solve this kind of problem.
Another serious problem that we face is shortage of land. By this I mean shortage of land suitable for housing, not farmable. It is not a good idea to convert good farmland to use for housing. I would prefer to see the kind of land that we have in northern Ontario used for housing, instead of land around the Niagara fruit district, which is
March 25, 1974

high-priced agricultural land. We cannot continue to use this kind of land for housing. Food production is going to be all important over the long term, which is why we must not use for housing land that is presently used for producing food.
As far as energy is concerned, we in Canada need a great deal of fuel to keep our houses warm. About 50 per cent of our consumption of energy is used to heat houses and buildings. In addition, the cost of energy is increasing and shortage of energy supplies over the long term is a matter that must be considered.
Let me say a word or two about demonstration projects. Last week I had the good fortune to attend the meeting of a group called the Castle Green Co-op. This is a group that is building 200 housing units and is funded by a bill passed in the last session of parliament that gives assistance to co-ops and co-op housing. About 100 people attended this meeting, all of them members of this particular co-op. I have never seen a more enthusiastic gathering at a straight grass-roots project. I am proud the project is in Thunder Bay and I am proud to be associated with the government that provided funds for the project. I spoke to this group-one of my shorter speeches-for about two minutes, outlining the Minister's proposal for demonstration projects.
I had not left this meeting for more than half an hour when I received a telephone call asking me whether I would meet the caller and talk about this project. We, that is, the people directing the project and myself, spent the better part of the night, until two or three in the morning, talking about the possibilities for this kind of project. We talked about extra funding for central heating, about locating housing to take full advantage of solar heat. We talked about closed sewage systems in areas where it was difficult to dispose of sewage. We talked of recycling garbage and using it to create energy for heating and cooling systems. We also talked about recreational activities and other things.
This kind of project is fascinating and is strictly grassroots. The whole idea of this demonstration project is to develop the grass-roots talent that we have. I explained to them very carefully that it was not a research project. If technological know-how is required, they will have to use technology already developed. But this does not mean we are not researching today projects that will be introduced four or five years from now.
I should like to say a few words about the cost of energy, not in terms of dollars and cents but in terms of the remaining energy resources of the world. I think this is what the people at the Castle Green Co-op meeting were talking about. The first thing that came to their minds was the question how to set up economic housing units in terms of energy cost in a cold part of the country, not as cold as the territories, perhaps, but nevertheless cold enough.
If we look at the energy demand curve in Canada as we double our population, the energy curve rises gently to start with but by about 1978 starts to go up and is almost perpendicular by 1982. This kind of curve is constant throughout the world. All energy curves are drawn in this way. On the other hand, supply curves tend to rise gently, and then between the years 1978 and 1982 or 1983, depend-
Urban Affairs
ing on how gentle or steep the curves are, they cross, which means that by 1983 at the latest we might be in for some serious trouble, especially if present demand continues.
My feeling is that we must do something to anticipate this, and this is why we should take another look at housing construction. Houses in a cold country require a lot of energy. Therefore, we should look at ways to cut this demand effectively now. That is what I think we can do with this particular program. In terms of developing countries, Canada stands forty-second or forty-ninth in relation to the efficient use of energy. We tend to use our energy in a very inefficient way; we waste a great deal of it. Sweden, on the basis of its population, uses only about half the energy per capita, with the same gross national product. I suggest we have a long way to go toward solving some of our energy demand problems. Just as an example of this problem, many of our commercial buildings are extremely wasteful in terms of energy use. I understand the Commerce Court building in Toronto uses the same amount of hydro as the city of Peterborough. This is the type of energy waste which we can no longer afford.
Many suggestions have been made, including some by the Castle Green Co-operative. One suggestion has to do with the better use of waste heat, that is, heat from 80 to 100 degrees from thermal nuclear generating plants. There are many ways of using this heat to create energy in various forms, and this is the kind of thing that must be done. Some of these things can be done under the demonstration project activities suggested by the minister.
Another suggestion relates to the use of garbage as a fuel. It has been found that a pound of garbage can be used to produce 4'/2 pounds of steam. I have not worked that out in terms of BTU's but it would be extremely significant. Another suggestion is that we use raw sewage for conversion into methane. Such a conversion project has been carried out in Toronto. This is something we should be looking into as the kind of project that should be funded. I understand that one industry in Toronto has established a plant at the Toronto stockyards to convert biomasses into methane.
There is also a fairly simple operation which allows the mixture of coal and oil, producing about the same flame with the same amount of heat one gets from using straight oil. Such an operation would have the effect of increasing the life expectancy of our oil reserves by about 33 per cent. I suggest there is a tremendous area in respect of alternate means of developing heat. Heat conservation is another area that must be examined. Various kinds of insulations should be developed and tested. We must also develop, examine and test various alternative and improved building materials.
Perhaps the shortages of conventional building materials, including wood, will reach the point where we will have to reconsider the effectiveness of conventional insulation. Perhaps it will be proved that we should not be burning all our oil, but should be converting it into plastics of various forms which are better building materials. Perhaps they can be produced in the planning sections of

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
our economy rather than in the market sections-produced much more efficiently with much better insulating qualities. These are some of the things I think can be done.
Having pointed out these things, let me say there is a very definite need to find new techniques if we are to double our housing needs in uiban centres in the next 25 years. This is not a matter of taking a new research approach but is a matter of demonstration projects. What we must do is use some of the technology that now exists. This same Toronto industry used existing technology in its conversion of sewage to methane. This is the kind of thing that can and must be done. We must use existing technology of this kind, perhaps in a model city or a community, in an effort to show how we can avoid this kind of waste. Perhaps then the proposed $20 million a year will be money well spent. If that is how it is intended we spend this money, I think the money will be well spent and I support such an expenditure for that reason.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to some of the comments of hon. members on the other side, including the minister. When the minister finished his speech I was quite convinced that there was no housing crisis in this country. He indicated that as a result of the many great things he is doing there is absolutely nothing else that can be done. I suggest this is the kind of rather negative attitude in respect of our housing situation which has created the severe problem which exists in Canada today.
I am inclined to think the minister has failed to take action of any kind in the area of providing additional serviced land and cutting down interest rates because the people involved in the financial institutions and development corporations which are making huge rakeoffs on serviced lands are friends of and contributors to his party. It is well known that the Liberals are in the pockets of these institutions and do not want to do anything to rock the boat too much.
The hon. member who preceded me made a good deal of fuss about new techniques and new ways of doing things. This is an indication of the fact that people on that side are living in a world of daydreams and are not really prepared to grapple with our problems, using the knowledge and information we have at hand, but are content to sit back and do nothing but suggest they are trying to think up new techniques to solve our problems.
The parliamentary secretary used the same old type of criticism we hear from Liberals all across the country. The only thing they can say about the Conservative Party is that we have no new policies. It is obvious that those hon. members have not done their homework or they were not in the House when the minister spoke. Anyone who had listened to him would have seen that the minister had a copy of our policy discussion paper in his hand when he spoke.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Perhaps while he is still temporarily the minister he will be able to implement some of the good ideas which are contained in that paper, which will go a long way toward salving some of our problems in respect of housing. In spite of the glowing terms used by the minister when he spoke about his housing policies, I think his record speaks for itself. The policies which have been in effect for the past 11 years of Liberal government have led us to the point where we are becoming a nation of renters with virtually no one able to afford his own home today, and the situation is getting much worse. Fewer people even dare to dream about owning their own home.
We do not have to look far to see what has happened in respect of the housing market this year. Let us look at the situation in Ottawa, where in the past five years the price of the average house has doubled. One of my hobbies is to follow fairly closely this market and I should like to give an example of what has happened in Ottawa. In the neighbourhood in which I live, a house was sold last April for $45,000 to $47,000. That house was resold about three months ago for $72,000, and it is now advertised for sale at $95,000. In less than a year this house has more than doubled in price.
With that kind of inflationary pressure, I do not understand how the minister can sit back and smugly say he is doing everything he possibly can, or that there is really no problem in respect of housing in this country. I think it is fair to say that if something is not done about the inflation we are experiencing, the housing situation will be aggravated severely. Conversely, if the housing market is not stabilized, this will contribute to inflation. Inflation breeds high housing costs, and high housing costs breed inflation. This is a cycle that has to be broken somehow.
We have also heard many members on the government side state over and over again that we do not have in this country the land required for housing. That is a strange statement. The fact is that this country has more land than any country in the world. It is presently a matter of not having a government which has a policy to service the land and make it available to Canadians at reasonable cost. When we think of the millions of acres of land presently unoccupied in Canada, we find it rather difficult to understand why a building lot in the city of Ottawa, which I believe is a typical community, should cost $35,000 or $40,000. I am referring to a lot which is perhaps 100 feet by 100 feet.
I saw an advertisement in the paper the other day concerning a lot with trees on it. That made it valuable. It was advertised at $75,000. This was a lot which would
March 25, 1974

contain a one-family dwelling. While this type of situation occurs, it is no wonder the price of housing is becoming out of reach of the ordinary Canadian. It might be useful to look at the cause of this difficulty. Part of the cause, no doubt, is the fact that a large part of the development is left entirely in the hands of the developers. In spite of the minister's statement that there is a huge land assembly program, I have no knowledge of such a program working very effectively anywhere in this country. I do not see any such program in Ottawa.
We have a situation, for example, where a developer might buy a section of land perhaps for $2,000 or $10,000 an acre. About a third of that land will be taken for parks, roads, lanes, and so on, and he will wind up with probably three or four building lots per acre which he will in turn sell for $30,000 or $35,000 a piece. These lots are not available to individuals but are simply used by the developer for the construction of houses which are sold at a huge profit.
Another thing which would seem to be contributing to the high cost of housing, on which the minister, did not touch, of course, is the speculation which is carried on in land. People buy land and hold it for a month, two months, or less, and by this method tie up whatever land is available, simply to resell it at a profit. I think the minister should loolc into this situation to see that reason is instilled into that part of the housing situation.
Although I am a believer in the private enterprise system, I think there are certain areas where this system becomes self-defeating and does not serve the public interest. I hate to say that, but it seems to be the case in so far as the availability of serviced lots for individuals wishing to build homes is concerned. Even though the minister says there is a land assembly program in operation, it just does not work. It is not making land available at cost or slightly above cost. The demand is still for higher than the supply at the present time. So I really wonder whether the minister is serious about his land assembly program. He seems to be quite satisfied to sit back and do nothing more. It seems more like political window-dressing.
Another aspect of the housing problem which is contributing to the high cost of housing is financing. Over the past decade we have seen varying rates of interest. In 1966-67 the rate was around 6 per cent. At that time, and with that kind of interest rate, there was no undue inflation. The financial institutions seemed to survive and did not fold up because of the low interest rate. Things seemed to go along pretty well. Now, however, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) tells us it is impossible to do anything about interest rates which are in the vicinity of 10 per cent and 11 per cent.
The present interest rates are a crushing burden on any home owner. It is almost impossible for most individuals to consider owning a home because of this burden. I think the fact that the minister continually refuses to consider taking action to lower the interest rate suggests that the Liberal Party is subject to a good deal of pressure from various financial institutions. It could be that they are sharing the pot. I do not know for sure, but this is a possibility and perhaps it is why they are not willing to take the kind of action necessary to reduce interest rates to a reasonable level.
Urban Affairs
Another thing which could be done with regard to the financial market is to ensure that a larger percentage of the funds available is allocated to single family housing. I think this would be a step in the right direction. An additional factor in the high cost of housing is building materials. In the past year or so there have been rapid increases in the cost of building materials. Builders in some cases will not even quote a price on a house before it is built because they do not know from day to day what will be the cost of the materials necessary to construct the house.
Inflation has been so rampant in the area of building materials that something must be done quickly. We should ensure an adequate supply of building materials. There are various ways to do this, including reduction of exports and increased production. Another method is the removal of the sales tax on building materials. The Liberal way is to tax everything to death, but I think at this point the Conservative way would be better; that is, remove this tax and give people a chance to have a breather so far as building materials costs are concerned.
Then there is the cost of labour. I believe it would be appropriate at this point to compliment labour, including the labour unions which I think have shown, in the face of absolutely uncontrolled inflation, a good deal of restraint in not seeking unusually high wage settlements and by continuing to do their jobs. Therefore, labour is not the most serious aspect in respect of housing costs at this time.
It may be that the most important thing we could consider in relation to housing is the quality of life which is provided by the various housing programs in the country. Research seems to have shown that the aim we must have is that every individual or family which wishes to have a home should be able to own a private, single-family dwelling as opposed to the various multiple dwellings now available. It is not necessary for me to go into the various advantages of this apart from saying there is no structure which leads an individual family to feel more at home and enjoy privacy than the single-family dwelling.
Perhaps there has been too much of a trend in recent days toward townhouses, condominiums and dwellings of that nature. No doubt this is a reaction to the shortage of houses-a reaction to a crisis. In its reaction to this crisis, the government does not seem to have given any thought to the quality of life actually produced by this type of multiple housing. So when looking at the housing situation we should not simply look at it in terms of numbers but also in terms of the kind of housing starts we produce.
If we look around Ottawa we see hundreds upon hundreds of townhouse structures. Just imagine what those places will look like 30 years from now. My prediction is that they are slums of the future. We have not learned from past experience of crowding too many people into small areas for the sake of expediency at present. It is true that when these units are new, they are attractive and fairly pleasant, but I know they are not what Canadian families want and the danger is great that in 20 or 30 years' time they will simply be slums with which a future government will have to cope. So I would like to see a trend away from building these townhouses and con-

March 25, 1974
Urban Affairs
dominiums that are now spotting the urban environment a little too frequently.
One of the other things I wanted to speak about was land development and the type of lots that are made available to people today. Almost all the new developments in the major cities of Canada consist of building lots without any back lanes. When we consider the quality of life about which we are so concerned, this is a serious omission, for several reasons. One of them is that children are forced to play in the streets if they want space to run outside the boundaries of their own lot. The other reason is that lack of a back lane leads to a highly unsatisfactory sanitary arrangement because there is no room for the storage of garbage and people are forced to store it inside their garages or their basements where it attracts flies to the building. They take it out to the front of the lot once a week and in the summertime when it attracts flies, this is very unsatisfactory.
The other thing that makes lots without back lanes not very useful is the fact that there is no access to the back yard for machinery. If an individual who owns the house wants to get into the back yard to put in a swimming pool, plant a tree, etc., he cannot do so because houses are built too close together and there is no access to the back. For these various reasons I think the national building policy should encourage communities to return to the old system of subdividing lots with the inclusion of back lanes or at least the inclusion of a 20-foot strip of publicly-owned land which is not fenced and which would provide a playground or access to backyards.
I have been told that part of the reason for building subdivisions with no back lanes is that we have too many European planners coming into the country who are accustomed to planning in conditions where there is a severe shortage of land, so they try to get the maximum use out of each acre, and the maximum number of lots. The other possibility is that we are leaving this planning too much in the hands of developers who, because of the profit motive, are interested in getting the maximum number of lots out of each acre of land which they are servicing. Whatever the case may be, I consider this to be a very unhealthy trend which will lead to a reduction in the quality of life that people enjoy in our new neighbourhoods.
Finally, I want to say that Canadians should realize that what has happened in the housing market in Canada did not happen by accident. It happened as a result of 11 years of Liberal policies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR CONSIDERATION OF GOVERNMENT'S URBAN AFFAIRS POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the very short time allotted to me I would like to point out some aspects of the housing situation as it exists in this country and particularly as it exists in my riding. In my

constituency the needs are not restricted to the urban areas where I am concerned with the increased cost of housing and land and a steady rise in population, adding a further strain to the existing difficulties. They are also felt in the rural areas where the government has done little or nothing in the past.
It is time that some interest was shown in order to bring adequate housing to those who have been cut off from the benefits of an urban society. Rural housing must be supported with generous rehabilitation loans and grants made available to co-operative and non-profit housing groups as well as low income families. CMHC rules as applied to rural housing must be made flexible to accommodate those who can least afford to comply with the standards necessary in order to qualify for financial assistance. CMHC policy toward the Indian people must also be made as flexible as possible because these are the people who deserve as much support as is possible in the field of housing. Inadequate housing and lack of concern in the past has contributed to poor and unsanitary housing conditions that are so obvious to those who have the responsibility of dealing with such conditions.
The federal government, with the support of the Conservatives, passed the residential mortgage financing act which was Bill C-135. This was supposed to provide the necessary funds for mortgage investments and supplement Bill C-133. However, that act meant that the supply and control of mortgage funds for residential housing will be determined by the free play of market forces. It will not ensure the availability of adequate mortgage funds for new and existing dwellings in rural areas as there is no provision for compulsory allocation of funds in these areas. It will not provide special housing for Indian people or those on low incomes. It is simply a means of attracting capital to an area where a good profit can be realized at the expense of the home buyer.
Therefore, it is important for the government to take the necessary steps and to assume responsibility for ensuring an adequate supply of mortgage funds at low interest rates, to determine housing requirements together with the provinces, and to set annual targets and obtain firm commitments from financial institutions to meet housing needs in this country. There is no excuse for inaction in an area of the Canadian economy where adequate shelter for all Canadians must be the primary objective of the federal government.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REGIONAL PAY DIFFERENTIALS-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO CORRECT
PUBLIC SERVICE-REGIONAL PAY DIFFERENTIALS-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO CORRECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his always kindly way, the venerable President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) said that my question on March 15 relating to regional pay inequalities in Canada was based on lack of knowledge. If he said so, then of course that must be the case because, after all, he is the head of the Treasury Board and his attitude on all matters relating to his department is above reproach. Or is it? Well, I may not have the learned gentleman's knowledge, but what I do have is some appreciation of what constitutes fair play and equity so far as his pay policies are concerned. So once more, as so many members of my party have done in the past, I want to bring to the attention of this House the inequitable and regressive attitude exhibited by this government toward the concept of equal pay for equal work for employees under Treasury Board jurisdiction.
The President of the Treasury Board has taken a militant and unprogressive stand in support of an entirely indefensible position. One might say that he, in his neanderthal way, has redoubled his efforts in this regard having lost sight of his objectives, which surely should be to do away, on a gradual basis, with the situation that exists in this country whereby employees under Treasury Board jurisdiction, whether they are nurses in New Brunswick or shipyard workers in Nova Scotia, are paid differently than their counterparts in other areas of Canada.
It is not realistic to bring about an absolute removal of wage disparity all across Canada at once because of the sudden disruption this could cause in a number of trades where economies of scale are at play. However, there is no doubt that our national economy can accept the philosophy of equal pay for equal work, which should be carried out in two basic steps. One step is immediate acceptance of equal pay increases so that disparity is not further increased. The second would be to commence immediately reduction of the existing differential so that it can be eliminated over a period of time.
I and others in my party have put on record the great differentials in pay with regard to nurses under federal jurisdiction. I am sure it is well known that the bitterness that these nurses felt, and still feel, has caused a considerable amount of justifiable concern to their representatives such as Mr. Phythian, Mr. Spruin and others in the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada who worked so hard on their behalf in trying to have the arbitral award dated October 16 of last year reviewed. The President of the Treasury Board, of course, resisted any such action.
The nurses' situation is deplorable, but there are many others; for example dockyard workers who suffer from the same sort of illogical disparity. Let us look at the status of dockyard employees in Canada under the existing agreement between the Treasury Board and the Federal Government Dockyards Trades and Labour Council, which expires on March 23 of next year. The differential in wages paid to dockyard workers in Nova Scotia and British Columbia, or to be more precise in Halifax and
Adjournment Debate
Esquimalt, is very substantial indeed, yet the cost of living in these two cities is practically identical.
The contract rate for machine-tending at level 3 is $4.31 at Halifax, and $5.03 at Esquimalt. A classification in which the federal government should be very interested in a sense, since its members are so very good at it, is that of manipulators. For manipulating, at Halifax the rate is $4.92, and at Esquimalt $5.56. There are greater differentials existing than the ones I have cited.
It is a very ironic situation which finds that in those parts of Canada which suffer most from unemployment, inflation and various other economic maladies, workers receive considerably less wages than workers in the more prosperous parts of the nation, both doing exactly the same work. While the President of the Treasury Board attempts to explain the validity and the equity of his position with regard to the foregoing, Mr. Speaker, perhaps at the same time he will explain why he and his government are permitting the federal civil service to expand by another 13,000 employees and why projected government spending for the year starting April 1, 1974, is up so dramatically.
He should also keep in mind that the estimates are double what they were six years ago and four times what they were ten years ago. Yet this minister said on CTV "Question Period," if I am quoting him correctly, that so far as the main estimates were concerned, the government's purchases of goods and services other than transfer payments are substantially the same in the current year as they were last year.
In spite of that, the President of the Treasury Board refuses, in the midst of all these expenditures such as $750 million to be paid to outside consultants to the civil service, which itself is costing the nation in excess of $4 billion, to allocate funds to correct this very inequitable pay policy which goes straight to the heart of regional inequality and basic fairness so far as working people are concerned. I doubt if he could get one provincial premier to support the stand he takes in this regard. But of course the government has never been too concerned about what the provinces think. When we look around this chamber and see the representation that the government has from most of the provinces in Canada, the results of its attitude are plain to see.
